sheets.heading: Constitutional Development (Company Rule & Crown Rule)
sheets.text:
Constitutional Development (Company Rule & Crown Rule)

• Regulating Act 1773: Established the first Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta (1774). First Chief Justice: Sir Elijah Impey.

• Charter Act 1813: First time provision made for spending at least ₹1 lakh per year on education of Indians; ended Company’s trade monopoly in India (except tea & China).

• Charter Act 1833: Made Governor-General of Bengal the first Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck). First Law Member of Governor-General’s Council → Macaulay. Section 87 first opened Company service to Indians without discrimination of religion, colour, etc.

• Charter Act 1853: First time separated legislative & executive functions of Governor- General’s Council; introduced open competition for Civil Services.

• Government of India Act 1858: Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.

• Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto): First time Indians associated with Viceroy’s & Governors’ Executive Councils. Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian Law Member of Viceroy’s Executive Council. Introduced separate electorate for Muslims (Lord Minto called “Father of Communal Electorate”).

• Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford):

o First time introduced direct elections. o First time made Central Legislature bicameral. o First time introduced dyarchy in provinces. o First time used the term “responsible government”.

• Government of India Act 1935:

o First time provided for an All-India Federation (never came into existence). o Introduced dyarchy at the Centre (never implemented) and abolished it in

provinces. o Established Federal Court (inaugurated 1 Oct 1937; first Chief Justice: Sir

Maurice Gwyer). o Separated Burma from India; created Sindh & Orissa as new provinces. o Residuary powers vested in Governor-General.

Constituent Assembly & Making of Constitution

• Idea of Constituent Assembly first put forward by M.N. Roy (1934).

• First formal demand by Swaraj Party (Ranchi conference, May 1934).

• Constituent Assembly constituted under Cabinet Mission Plan 1946.

• First meeting: 9 December 1946 (temporary President: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha).

• First permanent elected Chairman/President: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (11 Dec 1946).

• First nominated temporary Deputy Chairman: Frank Anthony.

• First permanent Vice-President: H.C. Mukherjee.

• Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 (5th meeting of 1st session); adopted 22 January 1947.

• First draft of the Constitution prepared by Constitutional Advisor B.N. Rau.

• Constitution adopted: 26 November 1949; fully came into force: 26 January 1950.

• Number of women members in Constituent Assembly: 15.

Interim Government (1946)

• Announced: 24 August 1946; took charge: 2 September 1946.

• Vice-President of Executive Council: Jawaharlal Nehru.

• First Finance Minister of Independent India: R.K. Shanmukham Chetty (some sources also mention John Mathai later).

Fundamental Rights, Schedules, Amendments

• First explicit demand for Fundamental Rights: Constitution of India Bill, 1895.

• First Amendment Act 1951: Added 9th Schedule; added clause (4) to Art. 15; restricted Art. 19 rights; added Arts. 31A & 31B.

• Ninth Schedule inserted by First Amendment.

• First Schedule lists States & Union Territories.

• Parliamentary form of government first introduced in Great Britain.

• Presidential form first formed in USA.

President, Vice-President, Council of Ministers

• First President of India: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (from Bihar).

• First Woman President: Pratibha Patil.

• First Tribal Woman President: Droupadi Murmu.

• First Vice-President: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan.

• First Deputy Prime Minister: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

• Indira Gandhi was the first Prime Minister who was a Rajya Sabha member at the time of appointment.

• First no-confidence motion: Moved by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Nehru’s government (3rd Lok Sabha, 1963).

Parliament

• First Speaker of Lok Sabha: G.V. Mavalankar (also first Speaker of Central Legislative Assembly in 1925).

• First Tribal Speaker of Lok Sabha: P.A. Sangma (1996).

• First General Election to Lok Sabha: 1951–52 (first session of 1st Lok Sabha: 13 May 1952).

• First joint sitting of Parliament: 1961 (Dowry Prohibition Bill).

• First actress nominated to Rajya Sabha: Nargis Dutt (1980).

• Leader of Opposition first recognised in Lok Sabha: 1969.

• Chamber of Princes (120 members) created under Act of 1919; first Chancellor: Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner.

• Estimates Committee constituted for the first time in 1950.

• Ethics Committee (Rajya Sabha) – first such committee by any Indian legislature – constituted 1997; Lok Sabha Ethics Committee first constituted 2000.

• Public Accounts Committee set up first in 1921 (under GoI Act 1919).

Judiciary

• Federal Court established under GoI Act 1935 (1 Oct 1937); first CJ: Sir Maurice Gwyer.

• First woman Judge of Supreme Court: Justice M. Fathima Beevi (1989); also first Muslim woman in higher judiciary.

• Doctrine of Judicial Review first propounded in USA (Marbury v. Madison, 1803).

• Basic Structure doctrine first propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

• Supreme Court first held Fundamental Rights amendable in Shankari Prasad case.

• First PIL considered: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979).

Governor & State Legislature

• First woman Governor of any State: Sarojini Naidu (Uttar Pradesh).

• First woman Chief Minister of any State: Sucheta Kripalani (Uttar Pradesh).

Centre-State Relations, Emergency, Finance Commission, Planning

• President’s Rule (Art. 356) first imposed: PEPSU (1953) / Punjab (1951 – sources vary slightly).

• First Finance Commission: Constituted 1951 / set up 1952 under K.C. Neogy (first Chairman).

• First Chairman of Planning Commission: Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru (ex-officio).

• First Deputy Chairman of Planning Commission: Gulzarilal Nanda.

• First Vice-Chairman of NITI Aayog: Arvind Panagariya.

• Inter-State Council first established: May/December 1990.

Lokpal, Commissions, Election Commission

• Institution of Ombudsman first created in Sweden (1809).

• First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) recommended Lokpal & Lokayuktas (interim report by Morarji Desai).

• First Lokpal Bill presented: 1968.

• First Lokpal of India: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose.

• Maharashtra – first state to introduce Lokayukta (1971/1972). Odisha – first to pass Lokayukta Act.

• First Chairman of National Human Rights Commission: Justice Ranganath Misra (1993).

• First Law Commission of Independent India (1955): Chairman M.C. Setalvad.

• Public Service Commission first established under GoI Act 1919 (1 Oct 1926).

• First Chief Election Commissioner: Sukumar Sen (1950–1958).

• First woman Chief Election Commissioner: V.S. Ramadevi.

• Voting age lowered to 18 by 61st Amendment; first exercised in 1989 General Election.

• VVPAT first used: Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland (4 Sept 2013).

Political Parties, Official Language, Panchayati Raj

• Political parties got constitutional recognition for the first time: 1985 (52nd Amendment – 10th Schedule / Anti-defection).

• First President of Bharatiya Jana Sangh: Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee.

• First President of BJP: Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1980).

• First Official Language Commission: 1955 under B.G. Kher.

• Tamil declared first Classical Language.

• First Municipal Corporation in India: Madras (1688).

• Panchayati Raj first inaugurated: 2 October 1959 in Nagaur (Rajasthan) by Nehru. Rajasthan first state; Andhra Pradesh second.

• Madhya Pradesh – first state to implement 73rd Amendment in true spirit.

• Community Development Programme (1952) was the first major rural development programme after independence; National Extension Service started 1953.

sheets.text:
Constituent Assembly

Fact Detail First idea M.N. Roy (1934) First formal demand Swaraj Party (Ranchi Conference, May 1934) Congress demand Officially demanded at Patna (May 1934); Nehru’s clear

statement in 1938 Accepted in principle August Offer, 1940 Final proposal for elected Assembly Cripps Mission (1942) Constituted under Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946

Composition & Election

• Total seats planned: 389 (296 British India + 93 Princely States)

• Representation ratio: 1 member per 10 lakh population

• British India seats: 292 from Governor’s provinces + 4 from Chief Commissioners’ provinces

• Elections held: July–August 1946 (indirect election by Provincial Legislative Assemblies)

• Result: Congress – 208, Muslim League – 73, Others – 15

• Not based on Adult Franchise (restricted franchise under GoI Act 1935 – tax, education, property)

• Indirect election (members elected by Provincial Assemblies)

• Princely States initially stayed away; started joining from third session (April 1947)

• Women members: 15

sheets.heading: Prime Minister
sheets.text:
Prime Minister

Constitutional Position

• Real Executive Head of the Union (President is the nominal/constitutional head).

• Head of the Council of Ministers.

• Leader of the majority party/coalition in the Lok Sabha.

• Article 74: Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President.

• Article 75: Appointment, tenure, responsibility, etc.

Appointment (Art. 75)

• Appointed by the President.

• Normally the leader of the majority party in Lok Sabha.

• Can be from Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha.

• Need not be a member of Parliament at the time of appointment (must become member within 6 months – Art. 75(5)).

Powers & Functions

1\. Head of Council of Ministers – selects, allocates portfolios, can ask any minister to

resign. 2. Link between President and Council of Ministers (Art. 78):

o Communicates all decisions of CoM to the President. o Furnishes information required by the President. o Submits matters for reconsideration of CoM if President so requires. 3. Leader of the Lok Sabha (Leader of the House). 4. Chief Spokesperson of the Government. 5. Chairman of important bodies:

o NITI Aayog (earlier Planning Commission) o National Development Council o National Integration Council o Inter-State Council o National Disaster Management Authority 6. Advises the President on:

o Appointment of other Ministers o Summoning & prorogation of Parliament o Dissolution of Lok Sabha o Declaration of Emergency (recommendation of Cabinet)

Collective Responsibility (Art. 75(3))

• Council of Ministers (including PM) is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

• If a No-Confidence Motion is passed → en re Council (including PM) must resign.

Size of Council of Ministers

• 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003:

o Total Ministers (including PM) shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of Lok

Sabha. o Same limit applies to States (including CM).

Fact Detail First Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru Longest serving Jawaharlal Nehru First woman PM Indira Gandhi First non-Congress PM Morarji Desai Only PM who was never an MP when appointed

(Conventionally rare; must get elected within 6 months) Deputy Prime Minister Not a constitutional post (only political) Oath of PM Administered by the President Resignation Addressed to the President

• President = Head of the State

• Prime Minister = Head of the Government

• PM is not responsible to Rajya Sabha (only to Lok Sabha).

• PM can be a member of Rajya Sabha (e.g., Indira Gandhi initially, Manmohan Singh).

Important Articles

• Art. 74 → Council of Ministers to aid & advise President

• Art. 75 → Other provisions as to Ministers (appointment, responsibility, etc.)

• Art. 78 → Du es of Prime Minister

• Art. 75(1A) → 15% limit (inserted by 91st Amendment)

sheets.heading: President
sheets.text:
President

Constitutional Position

• Article 52: There shall be a President of India.

• Article 53: Executive power of the Union is vested in the President (exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him).

• Nominal / Constitutional Head of the State (Real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister).

• First Citizen of India and symbol of unity, integrity and solidarity of the nation.

• Supreme Commander of the Defence Forces (Art. 53(2)).

Election (Art. 54 & 55)

• Indirect election by an Electoral College consisting of:

o Elected members of both Houses of Parliament o Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States o Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the Union Territories of Delhi

and Puducherry (added by 70th Amendment)

• Nominated members of Parliament and State Legislative Councils do not participate.

• System of Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote + Secret Ballot.

• Value of vote of MLA and MP is calculated to ensure uniformity among states and parity between Union and States.

• Disputes regarding election decided by the Supreme Court (final).

Qualifications (Art. 58)

1\. Citizen of India 2. Completed 35 years of age 3. Qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha 4. Does not hold any office of profit

Term, Resignation & Removal

• Term: 5 years (Art. 56)

• Eligible for re-election any number of times (Art. 57)

• Resignation addressed to the Vice-President

• Can be removed by Impeachment for violation of the Constitution (Art. 61)

o Charge can be preferred by either House o Special majority required in both Houses

o Only elected members of State Assemblies do not participate in impeachment

(they do vote in election)

Vacancy

• In case of death, resignation, removal or otherwise → Vice-President acts as President (Art. 65)

• If both offices vacant → Chief Jus ce of India (or senior-most Judge of SC) acts as President (President’s Succession Act)

Powers of the President

1\. Executive Powers

• Appoints: Prime Minister, other Ministers, Governors, Judges of SC & HC, CAG, Attorney General, UPSC Chairman & members, Election Commissioners, Finance Commission, etc.

• Appoints the Prime Minister (normally leader of majority party)

• Can seek information from the Prime Minister (Art. 78)

2\. Legislative Powers

• Integral part of Parliament (Art. 79)

• Summons, prorogues and dissolves Lok Sabha

• Addresses Parliament (Art. 87)

• Assents to Bills (Art. 111) – Absolute Veto, Suspensive Veto, Pocket Veto

• Promulgates Ordinances when Parliament is not in session (Art. 123)

• Nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha

3\. Judicial Powers

• Appoints Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts

• Power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, suspend or commute sentences (Art. 72)

• Can seek advisory opinion of Supreme Court (Art. 143) – not binding

4\. Emergency Powers

• National Emergency (Art. 352)

• President’s Rule / State Emergency (Art. 356)

• Financial Emergency (Art. 360)

5\. Military & Diplomatic Powers

• Supreme Commander of Armed Forces

• Declares war and concludes peace (on advice of CoM)

• Appoints Ambassadors and High Commissioners

Important Discretionary Powers (Limited)

• Appointment of Prime Minister in case of hung Parliament

• Dismissal of government that has lost majority

• Dissolution of Lok Sabha

• Pocket Veto

• Returning advice of Council of Ministers for reconsideration (once – 44th Amendment)

Fact Detail First President Dr. Rajendra Prasad Longest serving Dr. Rajendra Prasad (two terms) First Woman President Pratibha Patil (12th / 14th by tenure count) First Tribal President Droupadi Murmu (15th) Oath administered by Chief Justice of India Emoluments charged on Consolidated Fund of India Order of Precedence Rank 1

• President is Head of the State, not Head of the Government.

• Not directly elected.

• Nominated members do not vote in Presidential election.

• Can return a Bill only once (except Money Bill).

• Ordinance-making power is co-extensive with legislative power of Parliament.

sheets.heading: Vice-President
sheets.text:
Vice-President

Constitutional Position

• Article 63: There shall be a Vice-President of India.

• Second-highest constitutional office (next to the President in the Order of Precedence).

• Modelled on the American Vice-President.

• Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art. 64).

Election (Art. 66)

• Indirect election by an Electoral College consisting of:

o Members of both Houses of Parliament (elected + nominated).

• State Legislative Assemblies do NOT participate (major difference from Presidential election).

• Method: Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote + Secret Ballot.

• All doubts and disputes regarding election decided by the Supreme Court (Art. 71) – decision is final.

Qualifications (Art. 66(3))

1\. Citizen of India 2. Completed 35 years of age 3. Qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha 4. Does not hold any office of profit

Term, Resignation & Removal

• Term: 5 years (Art. 67)

• Eligible for re-election any number of times.

• Resignation addressed to the President.

• Can be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Art. 67(b)).

o No formal impeachment like the President. o 14 days’ notice required.

Functions

1\. Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha

o Presides over the sittings of Rajya Sabha.

o Has a casting vote in case of a tie. o Does not preside when a resolution for his removal is under consideration. 2. Acts as President (Art. 65)

o When the office of President falls vacant due to death, resignation, removal or

otherwise. o When the President is unable to discharge his functions (absence, illness, etc.). o Maximum period as Acting President: 6 months (election for new President must

be held within 6 months).

Salary & Emoluments

• Draws salary and allowances as Chairman of Rajya Sabha (not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India as Vice-President).

• When acting as President → en tled to salary, allowances and privileges of the President.

Important Differences: President vs Vice-President

Feature President Vice-President Electoral College MPs + MLAs of States &

UTs Only Members of Parliament Qualification for House Lok Sabha Rajya Sabha Removal Impeachment (both

Houses)

Resolution by Rajya Sabha + agreement of Lok Sabha Resignation to addressed

Vice-President President

Part of Parliament Yes (integral part) No

• First Vice-President → Dr. S. Radhakrishnan

• Longest-serving → Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (two terms)

• Only person to serve two full terms as Vice-President → Mohammad Hamid Ansari

• Oath administered by → President

• Does not take part in the election of the President as a nominated member? (Nominated MPs do vote in Vice-Presidential election)

o State MLAs do not vote in Vice-Presidential election. o Vice-President is not a member of either House of Parliament. o Not appointed by the President (he is elected). o Salary as Vice-President is not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

sheets.heading: Chief Minister
sheets.text:
Chief Minister

Constitutional Position

• Real Executive Head of the State (Governor is the nominal/constitutional head).

• Head of the State Council of Ministers.

• Leader of the majority party/coalition in the State Legislative Assembly.

• Article 163: Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Governor.

• Article 164: Appointment, tenure, responsibility, etc. of Ministers.

Appointment (Art. 164)

• Appointed by the Governor.

• Normally the leader of the majority party in the Legislative Assembly.

• Can be from Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council (if the state has one).

• Need not be a member of the State Legislature at the time of appointment (must become a member within 6 months).

Powers & Functions

1\. Head of Council of Ministers – selects ministers, allocates portfolios, can recommend

removal of any minister. 2. Link between Governor and Council of Ministers (Art. 167):

o Communicates all decisions of the CoM relating to the administration of the

affairs of the State and proposals for legislation to the Governor. o Furnishes information required by the Governor. o Submits for the consideration of the CoM any matter on which a decision has

been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council. 3. Leader of the House (Legislative Assembly). 4. Chief Spokesperson of the State Government. 5. Advises the Governor on:

o Appointment of other Ministers o Summoning & prorogation of the State Legislature o Dissolution of the Legislative Assembly

Collective Responsibility (Art. 164(2))

• Council of Ministers (including CM) is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State.

• If a No-Confidence Motion is passed → en re Council (including CM) must resign.

Size of Council of Ministers

• 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003:

o Total Ministers (including CM) shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the

Legislative Assembly. o Minimum strength in smaller states: 12 (including CM).

Fact Detail Appointment By the Governor Oath administered by Governor Resignation addressed to Governor First woman Chief Minister Sucheta Kripalani (Uttar Pradesh) First non-Congress CM E.M.S. Namboodiripad (Kerala, 1957) CM of Delhi / Puducherry Appointed by the President (Art. 239AA)

• Governor = Head of the State

• Chief Minister = Head of the Government

• CM is responsible only to the Legislative Assembly (not to the Legislative Council).

• Governor appoints CM, but CM advises on the appointment of other Ministers.

• In case of hung Assembly, Governor has discretionary power in appointing CM.

Important Articles

• Art. 163 → Council of Ministers to aid & advise Governor

• Art. 164 → Other provisions as to Ministers (appointment, responsibility, size limit)

• Art. 167 → Du es of Chief Minister as respects the furnishing of informa on to Governor

sheets.heading: Governor
sheets.text:
Governor

Constitutional Position

• Nominal / Constitutional Head of the State (Real executive is the Chief Minister + Council of Ministers).

• Article 153: There shall be a Governor for each State. (Same person can be appointed as Governor of two or more States – 7th Amendment).

• Article 154: Executive power of the State is vested in the Governor.

• Appointed by the President (Art. 155) by warrant under his hand and seal.

• Holds office during the pleasure of the President (Art. 156).

• Normal term: 5 years (can be removed earlier or continue longer).

Qualifications (Art. 157 & 158)

1\. Citizen of India 2. Completed 35 years of age 3. Should not be a member of Parliament or State Legislature (if he is, he must vacate the

seat) 4. Should not hold any office of profit

Appointment, Oath & Salary

• Appointed by the President.

• Oath administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court (Art. 159).

• Emoluments and allowances charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 202).

• When the same person is Governor of two or more States → salary shared in such proportion as the President may determine.

Powers of the Governor

1\. Executive Powers

• Appoints the Chief Minister and other Ministers (on advice of CM).

• Appoints Advocate-General, State Election Commissioner, Chairman & members of SPSC, etc.

• Can seek information from the Chief Minister (Art. 167).

• Can recommend President’s Rule under Article 356.

2\. Legislative Powers

• Integral part of the State Legislature (Art. 168).

• Summons, prorogues and dissolves the Legislative Assembly.

• Addresses the State Legislature (Art. 176).

• Assents to Bills, withholds assent, or reserves the Bill for the consideration of the President (Art. 200).

• Promulgates Ordinances when the Legislature is not in session (Art. 213).

• Nominates members to the Legislative Council (if the State has one) – 1/6th of total strength.

3\. Judicial Powers

• Power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, suspend or commute sentences (Art. 161) – only for offences against State laws.

• Appoints District Judges (in consultation with High Court).

4\. Discretionary Powers

• Appointment of Chief Minister in case of hung Assembly.

• Dismissal of Council of Ministers that has lost majority.

• Dissolution of Legislative Assembly.

• Reserving a Bill for the consideration of the President.

• Recommending President’s Rule (Art. 356).

• Special responsibility in certain States (e.g., Sixth Schedule areas, Tribal areas, etc.).

Special Provisions

• Fifth Schedule: Governor has special responsibility for Scheduled Areas. Submits report to the President.

• Sixth Schedule: Special powers regarding Autonomous District Councils.

• Immunity under Article 361: No criminal proceedings during term of office; civil proceedings only after 2 months’ notice.

Key Differences: Governor vs President

Feature President Governor Appointed by Electoral College President Term 5 years 5 years (pleasure of President) Removal Impeachment Pleasure of President Ordinance-making Art. 123 Art. 213 Pardoning power Art. 72 (all cases) Art. 161 (State laws only) Discretionary powers Very limited Comparatively more

• First woman Governor → Sarojini Naidu (Uttar Pradesh)

• First woman Governor of an independent State → Padmaja Naidu (West Bengal)

• Governor of J\&K was earlier called Sadr-e-Riyasat (changed to Governor in 1965).

• Contingency Fund of the State is operated by the Governor.

• Decision on disqualification of MLAs under Anti-Defection → Governor (on advice of Election Commission).

o Governor is not elected; he is nominated/appointed. o Holds office during the pleasure of the President, not the Chief Minister. o Can reserve a Bill for the President even if the Council of Ministers advises otherwise

(discretionary). o Not bound by the advice of Council of Ministers in all matters (has discretionary

powers).

sheets.heading: Loksabha – Members
sheets.text:
Loksabha – Members

Composition (Art. 81)

• Maximum strength: 552

o Not more than 530 members from the States (directly elected) o Not more than 20 members from the Union Territories o (Earlier provision for 2 nominated Anglo-Indian members under Art. 331 has

been discontinued by the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019)

• Present strength: 543 elected members (530 from States + 13 from UTs)

Qualification for Membership (Art. 84)

A person must be:

1\. A citizen of India 2. Not less than 25 years of age 3. Registered as a voter in any parliamentary constituency 4. Not hold any office of profit 5. Not of unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, etc. (as per Representation of the People

Act)

Disqualifications

• Under Art. 102 and Representation of the People Act, 1951

• Under Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) – decided by the Speaker

• If he becomes a member of both Houses → must choose one within 10 days

Term & Vacation of Seats

• Normal term: 5 years from the date of first sitting (Art. 83)

• Can be dissolved earlier by the President

• During National Emergency → can be extended by Parliament for 1 year at a me

• Seat becomes vacant on:

o Resignation (addressed to Speaker) o Disqualification o Absence for 60 days without permission o Becoming a member of the other House

Reservation of Seats (Art. 330)

• Seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population

• Reservation was initially for 10 years; repeatedly extended (last extended by 104th Amendment till 2030)

• Anglo-Indian nomination (Art. 331) → abolished after 25 January 2020

Fact Detail Minimum age 25 years Maximum strength 552 Present elected strength 543 Quorum 1/10th of total membership Resignation addressed to Speaker Decision on Anti-Defection Speaker First Lok Sabha strength 489 (elected) State with highest seats Uttar Pradesh (80)

Imp Articles

• Art. 81 → Composi on

• Art. 83 → Dura on

• Art. 84 → Qualifica on

• Art. 102 → Disqualifica on

• Art. 330 → Reserva on for SC/ST

• Art. 331 → Anglo-Indian (now discontinued)

• Art. 326 → Adult suffrage

⇨ Nominated Anglo-Indian members no longer exist (104th Amendment). ⇨ A person can contest from maximum two constituencies. ⇨ Minister who is not a member of Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha must get elected within 6

months. ⇨ Council of Ministers strength limited to 15% of total membership of Lok Sabha (91st

Amendment).

sheets.heading: Rajya Sabha – Members
sheets.text:
Rajya Sabha – Members

Composition (Art. 80)

• Maximum strength: 250

o Not more than 238 representatives of the States and Union Territories (elected) o 12 members nominated by the President

• Present strength: 245 (233 elected + 12 nominated)

• Only 3 Union Territories have representation: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir.

Mode of Election

• Indirect election by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies.

• System of Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote.

• Allocation of seats among States is based on population (Fourth Schedule).

• Nominated members: Persons having special knowledge or practical experience in Literature, Science, Art and Social Service.

Qualification (Art. 84)

A person must be:

1\. A citizen of India 2. Not less than 30 years of age 3. Registered as a voter in any parliamentary constituency 4. Not hold any office of profit 5. Other disqualifications same as Lok Sabha (Art. 102 + RPA, 1951 + Tenth Schedule)

Term • 6 years

• Permanent House → not subject to dissolution

• As nearly as possible, one-third of members retire every two years

• Casual vacancy filled for the remainder of the term

Special Powers of Rajya Sabha

1\. Art. 249: Can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in national interest

(2/3rd majority of members present & voting). 2. Art. 312: Can initiate creation of new All-India Services (2/3rd majority).

3\. Equal powers with Lok Sabha in Constitutional Amendment Bills. 4. Can introduce Ordinary Bills and Constitutional Amendment Bills.

Key Differences with Lok Sabha Members

Feature Rajya Sabha Lok Sabha Minimum Age 30 years 25 years Maximum Strength 250 552 Mode of Election Indirect Direct Term 6 years (permanent House) 5 years Dissolution Cannot be dissolved Can be dissolved Nominated Members 12 None (Anglo-Indian abolished) Money Bill Can only recommend (14 days) Introduces & has final say

Important Facts

• First nominated woman member → Nargis Du (1980)

• State with highest seats → U ar Pradesh (31)

• Quorum → 1/10th of total membership

• Resignation addressed to → Chairman (Vice-President)

• Decision on Anti-Defection → Chairman of Rajya Sabha

Imp Articles

• Art. 80 → Composi on

• Art. 83(1) → Dura on (permanent House)

• Art. 84 → Qualifica on

• Fourth Schedule → Alloca on of seats

• Art. 249 & 312 → Special powers

sheets.heading: Preamble
sheets.text:
Preamble

Source & Origin

• Based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947.

• Idea of Preamble borrowed from the Constitution of the USA.

• Language of the Preamble influenced by the Australian Constitution.

Text of the Preamble

WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens:

JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation;

IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

Keyword Meaning Sovereign Supreme authority; free from external control Socialist Added by 42nd Amendment (1976); aims at reducing inequality Secular Added by 42nd Amendment (1976); equal respect to all religions Democratic Government of the people, by the people, for the people Republic Head of the State is elected (not hereditary) Justice Social, Economic & Political Liberty Of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship Equality Of status and of opportunity Fraternity Assuring dignity of individual + unity & integrity of the Nation

Important Amendments

• 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (Mini Constitution):

o Added three words: Socialist, Secular, Integrity o Changed “Unity of the Nation” → “Unity and Integrity of the Na on”

• Preamble has been amended only once so far.

Judicial Status of Preamble

Case Year Ruling Berubari Union Case 1960 Preamble is not a part of the Constitution Golaknath Case 1967 Preamble is a part of the Constitution Kesavananda Case Bharati

1973 Preamble Basic Structure is a part cannot of the be Constitution destroyed

and can be amended, but

LIC of India Case 1995 Reaffirmed that Preamble is an integral part

• Preamble is the key to the Constitution / Soul of the Constitution / Political Horoscope (K.M. Munshi).

• It is non-justiciable (cannot be enforced in a court of law).

• It reflects the philosophy, ideals and objectives of the Constitution.

• Date mentioned in Preamble → 26 November 1949 (Date of Adoption).

• The word “Federal” is not mentioned in the Preamble.

• Three types of Justice → Social, Economic and Poli cal.

⇨ Preamble is a part of the Constitution (settled in Kesavananda Bharati). ⇨ It can be amended under Article 368, but Basic Structure cannot be altered. ⇨ Words “Socialist” and “Secular” were not originally present. ⇨ Preamble does not confer any power or create any right by itself.

sheets.heading: Fundamental Rights
sheets.text:
Fundamental Rights

• Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12 to 35)

• Borrowed mainly from the Bill of Rights of the USA

• First demand: Swaraj Bill (1895) → Mo lal Nehru Report (1928) → Karachi Session of Congress (1931)

Classification of Fundamental Rights (Originally 7, Now 6)

Right Articles Key Provisions 1. Right to Equality 14–18 Equality before law, prohibition of discrimination, opportunity, abolition of untouchability & titles

equality of

2\. Right to Freedom 19–22

Six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession), protection in respect of conviction, life & personal liberty, protection against arrest 3. Right against Exploitation 23–24 Prohibition of traffic in human beings & forced labour,

prohibition of employment of children in factories 4. Right to Freedom of Religion 25–28 Freedom of conscience, free profession, practice & propagation

of religion 5. Cultural & Educational Rights 29–30 Protection of interests of minorities, right of minorities to

establish & administer educational institutions 6. Right to Constitutional Remedies

Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of 32

Fundamental Rights (called the “Heart and Soul” of the Constitution by Dr. Ambedkar)

Note: Right to Property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 and made a legal right under Article 300-A.

Important Features

• Available against the State (Art. 12 defines State)

• Justiciable (enforceable by courts)

• Some rights available only to citizens (Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30)

• Some available to both citizens and foreigners (Arts. 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25–28)

• Can be suspended during National Emergency (except Arts. 20 & 21 after 44th Amendment)

• Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights but cannot destroy the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973)

Writs under Article 32 & 226

1\. Habeas Corpus – “To have the body” 2. Mandamus – “We command” 3. Prohibition – Issued by higher court to lower court 4. Certiorari – To quash the order of lower court 5. Quo-Warranto – “By what authority”

• Supreme Court → only for Fundamental Rights (Art. 32)

• High Courts → for Fundamental Rights + other purposes (Art. 226) → wider power

Landmark Cases

Case Year Importance Gopalan vs State of Madras 1950 Narrow interpretation of Art. 21 Golaknath Case 1967 Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights Kesavananda Bharati 1973 Parliament can amend FRs but not Basic Structure Maneka Gandhi Case 1978 Expanded scope of Art. 21 (due process) Minerva Mills Case 1980 Balance between FRs and DPSPs Indira Sawhney Case 1992 Reservation (Art. 16)

Suspension during Emergency

• Art. 358: Automatic suspension of Art. 19 during war/external aggression

• Art. 359: President can suspend enforcement of other FRs (except Arts. 20 & 21)

Imp Facts

• Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right

• Right to Education made Fundamental Right by 86th Amendment (Art. 21-A)

• Untouchability abolished under Art. 17

• Child labour prohibited under Art. 24

• Guardian of Fundamental Rights → Judiciary (Supreme Court & High Courts)

sheets.heading: Fundamental Duties
sheets.text:
Fundamental Duties

• Part → Part IV-A

• Article → Article 51-A

• Added by → 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976

• Recommended by → Swaran Singh Committee (1976)

• Inspired by → Cons tu on of the erstwhile USSR (Soviet Union)

• Originally → 10 duties

• Presently → 11 duties (11th duty added by 86th Amendment Act, 2002)

List of 11 Fundamental Duties (Art. 51-A)

It shall be the duty of every citizen of India —

(a) To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem

(b) To cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired our national struggle for freedom

(c) To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

(d) To defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so

(e) To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women

(f) To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture

(g) To protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures

(h) To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform

(i) To safeguard public property and to abjure violence

(j) To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement

(k) Who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years

(Added by 86th Amendment Act, 2002)

Key Features

• Non-justiciable (cannot be enforced by courts directly)

• Apply only to citizens (not to foreigners)

• No legal sanction for violation (but Parliament can make laws to enforce them)

• Help in interpreting ambiguous laws and determining the constitutionality of laws

Fact Detail Part IV-A Article 51-A Year of addition 1976 Amendment 42nd Committee Swaran Singh Original number 10 Present number 11 11th duty related to Education of children (6–14 years) Source USSR Constitution

Difference from Fundamental Rights

• Fundamental Rights → Jus ciable, available against the State

• Fundamental Duties → Non-justiciable, moral obligations on citizens

sheets.text:
Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)

• Part → Part IV of the Constitution

• Articles → 36 to 51

• Inspired by / Borrowed from → Irish Constitution

• Non-justiciable (cannot be enforced by any court) – Art. 37

• Fundamental in the governance of the country

• Aim → To establish Social and Economic Democracy and a Welfare State

Classification of Directive Principles

1\. Socialistic Principles

• Art. 38 → Promote welfare of the people & minimise inequalities

• Art. 39 → Adequate means of livelihood, equal pay for equal work, protec on of children, etc.

• Art. 39A → Equal jus ce and free legal aid (added by 42nd Amendment)

• Art. 41 → Right to work, educa on and public assistance

• Art. 42 → Just and humane condi ons of work & maternity relief

• Art. 43 → Living wage & decent standard of life

• Art. 43A → Par cipa on of workers in management of industries (added by 42nd Amendment)

• Art. 47 → Raise level of nutri on, standard of living and improve public health

2\. Gandhian Principles

• Art. 40 → Organisa on of Village Panchayats

• Art. 43 → Promote co age industries

• Art. 43B → Promo on of coopera ve socie es (added by 97th Amendment)

• Art. 46 → Promote educa onal & economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections

• Art. 47 → Prohibit consump on of intoxica ng drinks and drugs

• Art. 48 → Prohibit slaughter of cows, calves and other milch animals

3\. Liberal-Intellectual Principles

• Art. 44 → Uniform Civil Code

• Art. 45 → Early childhood care and educa on (originally free & compulsory educa on up to 14 years; amended by 86th Amendment)

• Art. 48 → Organisa on of agriculture and animal husbandry

• Art. 48A → Protec on and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife (added by 42nd Amendment)

• Art. 49 → Protec on of monuments and places of na onal importance

• Art. 50 → Separa on of Judiciary from Execu ve

• Art. 51 → Promo on of interna onal peace and security

Important Amendments Related to DPSP

Amendment Changes 42nd Amendment (1976) Added Art. 39A, 43A, 48A 44th Amendment (1978) Made Art. 38 more comprehensive (minimise inequalities) 86th Amendment (2002) Changed Art. 45 (education for children below 6 years) 97th Amendment (2011) Added Art. 43B (cooperative societies)

Key Differences: Fundamental Rights vs DPSP

Feature Fundamental Rights Directive Principles Nature Justiciable Non-justiciable Enforceability Can be enforced in courts Cannot be enforced in courts Aim Political Democracy Social & Economic Democracy Sanction Legal Moral & Political In case of conflict

Landmark Cases

• Champakam Dorairajan (1951) → FRs superior to DPSPs

• Golaknath (1967) → Parliament cannot amend FRs

• Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → Basic Structure

• Minerva Mills (1980) → Balance between FRs and DPSPs; both are equally important

Bills • Bill → Proposed legisla on; becomes an Act only after President’s assent under Art. 111

• Parliament consists of President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha (President is an integral part, not a member of either House)

• Ordinary Bill → Introduced in either House; both Houses hold equal legislative powers

• Money Bill → Introduced only in Lok Sabha with prior recommenda on of President; Rajya Sabha has recommendatory role only

• Constitution Amendment Bill → Introduced in either House; passed separately by each House by special majority; No Joint Sitting

Classification & Types of Bills

1\. Ordinary Bill (Art. 107, 108)

• Introduced in either House (Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha)

• Passed by simple majority; joint sitting (Art. 108) possible in case of deadlock

• Rajya Sabha has no fixed constitutional time limit to consider it

2\. Money Bill (Art. 109, 110)

• Introduced only in Lok Sabha with prior recommendation of President

• Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days (cannot amend or reject)

• Lok Sabha Speaker’s decision under Art. 110(3) is final; No Joint Sitting

• Includes taxes, borrowings, custody of/withdrawal from Consolidated Fund; does not include mere fines/penalties

3\. Financial Bill (I) — Art. 117(1)

• Contains matters of Art. 110 + general legislation

• Introduced only in Lok Sabha on President's recommendation

• Rajya Sabha has full power to reject/amend; Joint Sitting is possible

4\. Financial Bill (II) — Art. 117(3)

• Involves expenditure from Consolidated Fund of India without Art. 110 matters

• Introduced in either House; President's recommendation needed before consideration; Joint Sitting is possible

5\. Constitution Amendment Bill (Art. 368)

• Introduced in either House (no prior recommendation needed; cannot originate in State Legislature)

• Passed by each House separately by Special Majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting)

• Certain federal provisions require ratification by ≥ 1/2 State Legislatures

• No Joint Sitting; President shall give assent (no veto)

sheets.heading: Acts
sheets.text:
Acts

Company Rule: Key Acts (1773–1853)

• Regulating Act, 1773: Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings); Supreme Court established at Calcutta (1774, Chief Justice Elijah Impey); banned private trade/bribes.

• Pitt’s India Act, 1784: Established Dual Control Board of Control (Political affairs) + Court of Directors (Commercial affairs).

• Act of 1786: Governor-General empowered to override his Council and assume powers of Commander-in-Chief (first enjoyed by Lord Cornwallis).

• Charter Act, 1813: Abolished Company trade monopoly in India except for Tea and China trade; permitted Christian missionaries; allocated ₹1 lakh annual grant for Indian education.

• Charter Act, 1833: Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck); Company lost commercial status entirely; added 4th member as Law Member (Macaulay); Section 87 barred discrimination in Company service.

• Charter Act, 1853: First clear separation of Legislative and Executive functions of Governor-General’s Council; introduced Open Competition for Civil Services.

Crown Rule & Council Reforms (1858–1947)

• Government of India Act, 1858: Transferred rule from Company to British Crown; Governor-General designated as Viceroy (Lord Canning); abolished Board of Control/Court of Directors; created Secretary of State for India (assisted by 15-member Council).

• Indian Councils Act, 1861: Restored legislative powers of Bombay and Madras (decentralization); initiated Indian participation in law-making; introduced Portfolio System and Viceroy's Ordinance Power (max 6 months).

• Indian Councils Act, 1892: Permitted discussion on Budget and addressing questions to executive (6 days prior notice); supplementary questions and budget voting were not allowed; introduced indirect election principle.

• Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms): Introduced Separate Electorates for Muslims; allowed supplementary questions; first Indian appointed to Viceroy’s Executive Council (Satyendra Prasad Sinha).

• Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms): Introduced Dyarchy in Provinces; introduced Direct Elections and Bicameralism at Centre; separated Central and Provincial budgets; established the Chamber of Princes.

• Government of India Act, 1935: Introduced Provincial Autonomy (abolished provincial dyarchy); proposed (unimplemented) All-India Federation and Central Dyarchy;

established Federal Court (1937, CJ Maurice Gwyer); basis for President’s Ordinance Power (Art. 123).

• Indian Independence Act, 1947: Ended British sovereignty; created two independent Dominions (India and Pakistan); Constituent Assemblies given dual constitution-making and legislative powers.

Key Constitutional Amendment Acts

• 42nd Amendment (1976): "Mini-Constitution"; inserted Fundamental Duties (Part IVA / Art. 51A); added Socialist, Secular, Integrity to Preamble.

• 44th Amendment (1978): Nullified emergency-era distortions; restored fundamental safeguards.

• 52nd Amendment (1985): Enacted Anti-Defection Law; inserted the 10th Schedule (amended Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191).

• 73rd & 74th Amendments (1992): Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj (Part IX, Arts. 243–243O, 3-tier system) and Municipalities (Part IXA, Arts. 243P–243ZG).

• 84th Amendment (2001): Froze Lok Sabha seat allocations based on the 1971 Census up to the year 2026.

• 86th Amendment (2002): Inserted the 11th Fundamental Duty under Art. 51A(k) regarding education of children.

• 91st Amendment (2003): Strengthened anti-defection provisions and limited council of ministers' size.

• 99th Amendment (2014): Created National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC); declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 2015.

Major Governance & Statutory Acts

• Representation of the People Act, 1950: Framework for seat allocation, electoral rolls, and Legislative Council composition (Sec. 10 / Sched. 3 / Art. 171).

• Representation of the People Act, 1951: Registration of political parties by ECI; conduct of elections; disqualification upon conviction (≥ 2 years imprisonment disqualified during term + 6 years post-release).

• Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993: Enforced on 28 Sept 1993; established NHRC, SHRCs, and Human Rights Courts for life, liberty, equality, and dignity.

• Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005: Assented 15 June 2005, effective 12 October 2005; legal right supporting transparency/accountability (Namit Sharma Case, 2012; rooted in MKSS movement).

• Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: 5-member Selection Committee (PM as Chair, LS Speaker, LS LoP, CJI/SC nominee, Eminent Jurist; Rajya Sabha Chairman is NOT a member); min age 45 years; covers PM and public servants inside/outside India.

Imp Facts

• 1861 vs 1935 (Ordinance): Viceroy's Ordinance power originates in the Indian Councils Act, 1861, whereas Art. 123 of the Indian Constitution is modeled after Section 42 of the GoI Act, 1935.

• 1813 vs 1833 (Monopoly): Trade monopoly in India was partially abolished in 1813 (retained Tea + China) and completely abolished in 1833.

• 1919 vs 1935 (Dyarchy): Provincial Dyarchy = 1919; Central Dyarchy proposed = 1935.

• High Courts Act, 1861: High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras established in 1862.

• Social/Security Acts: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (23 sections, effective 1990); PWDVA, 2005 (effective 2006); MISA, 1971 was an internal security statute, not a social welfare act.

sheets.heading: Constitutional Amendments
sheets.text:
Constitutional Amendments

• Article 368 (Part XX) governs the amendment powers and procedure of the Indian Constitution, balancing flexibility and rigidity.

• 3 Methods of Amendment:

o Simple Majority (Outside Art. 368): Creation/alteration of States (Art. 3),

creation/abolition of State Legislative Councils (Art. 169), salaries of judges/officials. o Special Majority (Under Art. 368): Passed by each House separately by a

majority of the total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting. o Special Majority + Ratification by ≥ 1/2 State Legislatures: Required for federal

provisions (e.g., Presidential election, Union/State executive & legislative relations, Supreme Court & High Courts, 7th Schedule Lists, Art. 368 itself, GST Council).

Crucial Rules

• Initiation: Constitution Amendment Bill can originate in either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (cannot be introduced in State Legislatures).

• Prior Recommendation: Prior recommendation of the President is NOT required.

• No Joint Sitting: Each House must pass the Bill independently with special majority; if one House rejects it, the Bill fails completely.

• Presidential Assent: President must give assent (no veto/return power; made mandatory via 24th Amendment, 1971).

• Federal Ratification List: Requires ratification by simple majority of ≥ 1/2 States (not all States). First amendment requiring State ratification was the 3rd Amendment, 1954 (Entry 33, Concurrent List).

o Trap: Qualifications, conditions of office, and tenure of the President do NOT

require State ratification.

Imp Amendments

Added right to form Co-operative Societies (Art. 19(1)(c)), DPSP Art. 43B, and Part IX-B (Arts. 243ZH–243ZT; max 21 directors under Art. 243ZJ).

created GST Council (Art. 279A).

their own SEBCs (Socially and Educationally Backward Classes).

Schedules & Parts Added by Amendments

• 9th Schedule: Added by 1st Amendment (1951) -- Validation of certain Acts/Regulations (Land reforms).

• 10th Schedule: Added by 52nd Amendment (1985) -- Anti-Defection provisions.

• 11th Schedule: Added by 73rd Amendment (1992) -- 29 Functional items for Panchayats.

• 12th Schedule: Added by 74th Amendment (1992) -- 18 Functional items for Municipalities.

• Part IV-A: Added by 42nd Amendment (1976) -- Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A).

• Part IX-A: Added by 74th Amendment (1992) -- Municipalities (Arts. 243P–243ZG).

• Part IX-B: Added by 97th Amendment (2011) -- Co-operative Societies (Arts. 243ZH– 243ZT).

Imp Facts

• 42nd vs 44th (Advice to President): 42nd made CoM advice completely binding; 44th gave President one opportunity to return advice for reconsideration.

• 52nd vs 91st (Defection & Ministry Size): 52nd introduced anti-defection disqualification; 91st barred defectors from becoming ministers and enforced the 15% ministry ceiling.

• 86th vs 93rd (Education): 86th created the fundamental right to elementary education (Art. 21A, 6–14 yrs); 93rd enabled OBC reservation in higher education admissions.

• Note: o 13th Amendment: Created special provisions for Nagaland (Art. 371A).

o 83rd Amendment (2000): Exempted Arunachal Pradesh from reservations for

Scheduled Castes in Panchayats.

sheets.heading: Imp Cases
sheets.text:
Imp Cases

Amendment Power & Basic Structure Chain

• Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951): Upheld Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights under Art. 368.

• Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965): Reaffirmed that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.

• Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967): Reversed earlier rulings; held that Parliament CANNOT amend Fundamental Rights (first time Parliament's amending power was limited).

• Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): 13-Judge Bench propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine; held Parliament can amend FRs but cannot alter/destroy the Basic Structure; recognized the Preamble as part of the Constitution.

• Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Reinforced the Basic Structure doctrine; struck down clauses giving absolute precedence to DPSPs over FRs; restored the balance between Part III and Part IV.

Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases

• A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950): Narrow interpretation of Article 21; focused on "procedure established by law" concerning preventive detention.

• Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Held that in case of conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs; led directly to the 1st Constitutional Amendment, 1951 (inserted Art. 15(4) for reservations).

• Berubari Union Case (1960): Held that the Preamble is NOT an integral part of the Constitution (later overturned by Kesavananda Bharati and S.R. Bommai).

• Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): Struck down parts of the 39th Amendment that barred judicial review of election disputes of the PM and Speaker.

• Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): Widened Article 21 (Right to Travel Abroad); procedure must be "just, fair, and reasonable"; established the golden triangle (Arts. 14, 19, and 21 are mutually inclusive).

• P. Sambamurthy v. State of A.P. (1987): Challenged and struck down portions of the 32nd Constitutional Amendment.

• Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillu (1993): Upheld the validity of the 52nd Amendment (10th Schedule - Anti-Defection Law); held that Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review.

• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): Laid guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356 (President's Rule); made proclamation subject to judicial review; held secularism and federalism as basic features; reaffirmed Preamble as an integral part.

sheets.heading: Election Commission
sheets.text:
Election Commission

• Constitutional Status: Permanent, independent, constitutional body under Part XV (Articles 324–329).

• Established on 25 January 1950 (celebrated annually as National Voters' Day since 2011).

• Article 324(1): Vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission of India (ECI).

• Mandate covers elections to: Parliament (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), State Legislatures (Assemblies & Councils), President, and Vice-President.

• Local body elections (Panchayats and Municipalities) are NOT conducted by ECI; they fall under the State Election Commission (SEC) under Articles 243K & 243ZA.

Composition, Appointment & Removal

• Composition: 1 Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) + 2 Election Commissioners (multi- member body established continuously since 1 October 1993). All three have equal powers, salary equivalent to Supreme Court Judges, and decide by majority.

• Appointment: By the President of India.

• Tenure: 6 years or up to 65 years of age, whichever is earlier.

• Removal Safeguards:

o CEC: Removed only in like manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court

Judge (Art. 324(5)). o Other ECs & Regional Commissioners: Removed by the President on the

recommendation of the CEC.

Core Functions, Disqualifications & Powers

• Electoral Rolls & Suffrage:

o Art. 325: Single general electoral roll; no discrimination based on religion, race,

caste, or sex. o Art. 326: Universal Adult Suffrage for Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies. o Voting Age: Reduced from 21 to 18 years via the 61st Amendment Act, 1988

(effective 1989). o Nature of Right to Vote: A Legal/Statutory Right (Kuldip Nayar Case), not a

Fundamental Right.

• Disqualification Role:

o MPs (Art. 103): Decided by the President based on the binding opinion of the

ECI. o MLAs/MLCs (Art. 192): Decided by the Governor based on the binding opinion

of the ECI.

• Party Registration & Symbols: Registers political parties under RPA 1951; allots symbols and decides recognition under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968; adjudicates party merger/split disputes.

• Model Code of Conduct (MCC): Formulated and enforced by ECI from the date of election schedule announcement (ECI-formulated guideline, NOT an Act of Parliament).

National Party Criteria (Any One Condition)

• ≥2% of Lok Sabha seats won from at least 3 different States, OR

• ≥6% of valid votes polled in Lok Sabha/Assembly elections in ≥4 States + at least 4 Lok Sabha seats, OR

• Recognized as a State Party in at least 4 States.

Imp Facts

• Notification: Election notifications are issued by the President (Parliament) or Governor (State Legislature)—NOT by the ECI. ECI only recommends dates and determines the schedule.

• Delimitation Commission vs ECI: Constituency delimitation is executed by an independent Delimitation Commission set up under parliamentary law, whose orders cannot be questioned in court or modified by legislatures.

• Candidature Limits (RPA 1951, Sec. 33): A candidate can contest from a maximum of 2 constituencies (Lok Sabha or State Assembly).

• Forfeiture of Security Deposit: Occurs if a candidate fails to secure more than 1/6th of total valid votes polled.

• Election Reforms Chronology: EVM (1982, Parur, Kerala) → EPIC Voter ID (1993) → VVPAT (Sept 2013, Noksen, Nagaland) → NOTA (Sept 2013).

• Key Personalities: Sukumar Sen (1st CEC, 1950–58); V. S. Ramadevi (1st Woman CEC, 1990).

• Simultaneous Elections (ONOE) Articles: Potentially requires amending Arts. 83, 85, 172, 174, and 356.

sheets.heading: Finance Commission
sheets.text:
Finance Commission

• Constitutional Status: Permanent, independent, quasi-judicial constitutional body under Article 280 (Part XII).

• Constituted by the President of India every 5 years or earlier as deemed necessary (not strictly/rigidly every 5 years).

• First Commission: Constituted under Presidential order in 1951, set up on 6 April 1952 under Chairman K.C. Neogy.

• Core Function: Anchor of Fiscal Federalism; recommends the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Union and States, and the allocation among States.

Composition & Qualifications

• Composition (Art. 280(1)): Total 5 members → 1 Chairman + 4 other members appointed by the President.

• Qualifications (Art. 280(2)): Determined by Parliament by law (NOT determined by the President or Union Cabinet).

• Nature: Possesses powers of a civil court regarding summoning and production of documents (quasi-judicial character).

Core Functions (Art. 280(3)) & Report Submission (Art. 281)

• Devolution of Taxes: Distribution of the net proceeds of divisible Union taxes between Centre and States, and allocation among States.

• Grants-in-Aid: Principles governing grants-in-aid of State revenues out of the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 275).

• Local Bodies Resource Augmentation: Measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities based on recommendations of the State Finance Commission.

• Sound Finance: Any other matter referred to it by the President in the interest of sound public finance.

• Submission of Report (Art. 281): Submits its report to the President, who causes it to be laid before both Houses of Parliament along with an explanatory memorandum on action taken ( Trap: Report is laid by the President, NOT the Finance Minister).

sheets.heading: National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)
sheets.text:
National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)

• Statutory Identity: Statutory, independent body established under the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993 (Effective from 28 September 1993).

• It is a Statutory body, NOT a Constitutional body.

• Definition of Human Rights: Rights relating to Life, Liberty, Equality, and Dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants and enforceable by courts in India.

• Institutional Hierarchy under PHRA 1993: NHRC (National level) → SHRC (State level) → Human Rights Courts (District/Trial mechanism for speedy trials).

Composition & High-Level Selection Committee

• Composition: Chairperson (former Chief Justice of India/SC Judge) + judicial/expert members and specified ex-officio representation.

• Appointing Authority: Appointed by the President of India based on the recommendations of a 6-member High-Level Selection Committee.

Selection Committee Composition :

• Chairperson: Prime Minister

• Members:

o Speaker of Lok Sabha o Union Home Minister o Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha o Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha o Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha

• Trap: The Chairman of Rajya Sabha is NOT a member of the Selection Committee (Deputy Chairman represents the Rajya Sabha).

• Nature of Recommendations: Recommendations are advisory/recommendatory in nature; it does not act as a regular court of law or execute criminal sentencing directly.

• Armed Forces Jurisdiction Trap (Section 2(m)):

o NHRC does NOT have direct/unrestricted investigative powers over armed

forces. o Under the statutory procedure, it calls for an independent report from the

Central Government and makes recommendations based on that report.

• Section 2(m): Defines Armed Forces under the Act (includes naval, military, and air forces + other Union armed forces).

sheets.heading: Lok Sabha: Rules of Procedure & Conduct of Business
sheets.text:
Lok Sabha: Rules of Procedure & Conduct of Business

• The Constitution provides the broad institutional framework; day-to-day proceedings in Lok Sabha are governed by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.

• Crucial Exam Distinction: Several major parliamentary tools (e.g., No-Confidence Motion, Zero Hour, Rule 377) are NOT mentioned in the Constitution—they derive from Rules or procedural conventions.

• Primary mechanisms for executive accountability: Question Hour, Supplementary Questions, and Adjournment Motions.

Motions & Important Rules

• No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198):

o Not mentioned in the Constitution; introduced ONLY in Lok Sabha. o Moved against the entire Council of Ministers (cannot be moved against an

individual minister). o Requires written notice to the Secretary-General and the support of at least 50

members for leave to be granted.

• Confidence Motion: Moved by the Council of Ministers/Government to demonstrate majority support on the floor.

• Rule 184 (Discussion + Voting): Permits discussion on a specific matter of public interest followed by voting (carries significant political consequences for the government).

• Rule 377 (Special Mention of Matters): Allows members to raise matters of general public importance that cannot be raised under rules governing Questions, Calling Attention, or other formal Motions; requires written notice and Speaker's consent (increased from 20 to 30 matters/day in 2015).

• Rule 8(1): Governs the procedure for the election of the Deputy Speaker (date fixed by the Speaker and notified by the Secretary-General).

Feature Question Hour Zero Hour

Types of Parliamentary Questions

• Starred Question: Requires an oral answer on the floor; supplementary questions are ALLOWED (max 20 starred questions listed for oral answer per day).

• Unstarred Question: Requires a written answer laid on the table; supplementary questions are NOT allowed.

• Short Notice Question: Pertains to an urgent matter of public importance; asked with notice shorter than 10 clear days; receives an oral answer; supplementary questions are ALLOWED.

Debate Regulation & Other Motions

• Adjournment Motion:

o Interrupts normal business to discuss a definite matter of urgent public

importance and recent occurrence. o Involves an element of censure/condemnation against the government.

• Calling Attention Motion:

o Indian parliamentary innovation to draw the attention of a Minister to an

urgent matter of public importance.

o Resembles an Adjournment Motion but does NOT contain an element of

censure/condemnation.

• Closure Motion & Guillotine:

o Closure Motion: Moved to cut short debate and put the question to vote. o Guillotine: A form of closure applied when allotted time expires all remaining discussed and undiscussed clauses/demands are immediately put to vote.

Important Facts:

• Article vs Rule Matching:

o No-Confidence Motion: Lok Sabha Rule 198 (NOT an Article). o Rule 184: Substantive motion requiring discussion with voting. o Money Bill / Joint Sitting: Constitutional (Arts. 110 & 108).

• Negative Traps:

o Zero Hour is NOT a constitutional provision. o No-Confidence Motion can NOT be moved in Rajya Sabha. o Unstarred questions do NOT allow supplementary questions. o Calling Attention does NOT carry censure/condemnation against the

government.

Chief Justice & Supreme Court

• Constitutional Status: Head of the Union Judiciary and the Supreme Court of India under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147).

• Appointment: Appointed by the President of India under Article 124(2); by convention, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court is appointed as Chief Justice of India (CJI).

• Tenure & Retirement: Holds office until attaining the age of 65 years (no fixed term in years).

• Oath: Administered by the President (or a person appointed by the President) under the Third Schedule.

• Resignation: Addressed in writing to the President of India.

Appointment, Collegium & Removal Procedures

• Collegium Evolution:

o First Judges Case (1981): "Consultation" does not mean "concurrence";

executive supremacy in judicial appointments. o Second Judges Case (1993): "Consultation" means "concurrence"; introduced

the Collegium system (CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges). o Third Judges Case (1998): Expanded the Collegium to CJI + 4 senior-most SC

judges for SC appointments. o 99th Amendment & NJAC (2014–15): National Judicial Appointments

Commission struck down as unconstitutional to preserve the Independence of the Judiciary (Basic Structure).

• Removal Procedure (Art. 124(4)):

o Removed by an order of the President after an address by Parliament. o Grounds: Proved misbehaviour or incapacity. o Majority Required: Special Majority in each House (majority of total

membership + ≥ 2/3 of members present and voting in the same session). o Governed procedurally by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.

Key Jurisdictional Powers of the Supreme Court

• Original Jurisdiction (Art. 131): Exclusive jurisdiction over federal disputes (Centre ↔ State or State ↔ State). Does not cover pre-Constitution treaties or inter-State water disputes (Art. 262).

• Writ Jurisdiction (Art. 32): Fundamental Right to approach the SC directly for enforcement of Part III rights (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo- Warranto).

• Advisory Jurisdiction (Art. 143):

o On question of law/public importance: SC may tender or refuse advice. o On pre-Constitution disputes: SC is bound to give advice. o In all cases, the advice tendered is not binding on the President.

Procedural Distinctions

• Acting CJI vs Ad Hoc Judge:

o Acting CJI (Art. 126): Appointed by the President when the CJI is unable to

perform duties. o Ad Hoc Judge (Art. 127): Appointed by the CJI (with previous consent of the

President and consultation with the concerned HC Chief Justice) to meet a lack of quorum.

• Removal vs Appointment: The President appoints SC judges in consultation/collegium concurrence, but removal requires a statutory inquiry + parliamentary special majority address under Art. 124(4).

• Court of Record (Art. 129): Judgments have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any subordinate court; includes power to punish for contempt.

sheets.heading: Attorney General of India
sheets.text:
Attorney General of India

• Constitutional Status: Highest law officer of the Government of India under Part V (Article 76).

• Appointment: Appointed by the President of India.

• Tenure: Holds office during the pleasure of the President (No fixed constitutional tenure).

• Removal & Resignation: Can be removed at any time by the President; resignation is submitted to the President (traditionally resigns when the Council of Ministers changes).

• Remuneration: Determined by the President (not fixed by Parliament or the Constitution).

• Primary Role: Advises the Government of India on legal matters and performs other legal duties referred by the President.

Qualifications & Rights of Audience

• Qualifications (Equivalent to a Supreme Court Judge):

o Must be a citizen of India, AND o Has been a High Court Judge for at least 5 years, OR o Has been an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years, OR o Is a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President.

• Right of Audience: Enjoys the right of audience in all courts within the territory of India while performing official duties.

Question Hour & Related Hours  
 
Core Mandate: Primary parliamentary instruments to enforce executive accountability



o Requires a Written Answer laid on the table. 
o Supplementary questions are NOT allowed. 
 
Short Notice Question: 
o Relates to a matter of urgent public importance. 
o Asked with shorter notice than the standard prescribed period. 
o Receives an oral answer; supplementary questions are ALLOWED.

Election Machinery: 
o Election Commission of India (Art. 324): Conducts elections for President, Vice-





(Presidential/Vice-Presidential disputes handled exclusively by the Supreme Court 
under Art. 71)—NOT by ECI.

the grounds that vacancies exist in the electoral college (Art. 71(4)). 
 
Vote Value: MLA vote value varies from State to State based on population ratios; MP 
vote value is uniform across all MPs.

sheets.heading: Local Self-Government
sheets.text:
Local Self-Government    
 
Core Principle: Exercise in democratic decentralisation, community participation, and 
local accountability (NOT central control or mere administration). 
 
Constitutional Directive: Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organize Village 
Panchayats as units of self-government.  
 
Historical Landmarks: 
o Charles Metcalfe: Described Indian village communities as "Little Republics". 
o Lord Ripon (1882 Resolution): Recognized as the Father of Local Self-
Government in India. 
o GoI Act, 1919: Local Self-Government made a Transferred Subject under 
provincial dyarchy. 
o First Panchayati Raj State: Rajasthan (Nagaur District on 2 October 1959), 
followed second by Andhra Pradesh. 
o First Municipal Corporation: Madras (1688). 
Evolution: Landmark Committees 
 
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957): Recommended 3-tier Panchayati Raj (Gram 
Panchayat  -- Panchayat Samiti  -- Zila Parishad); recognized as the Architect of 
Panchayati Raj. 
 
Ashok Mehta Committee (1977–78): Recommended a 2-tier model and separate Nyaya 
Panchayats. 
 
Hanumantha Rao Committee (1983): Decentralisation of powers/finance and district 
planning bodies. 
 
G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985): Revitalization and representative character of 
Panchayats. 
 
L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986): Recommended constitutional status and greater 
financial resources for local bodies.

Imp Articles  
 
Art. 243A (Gram Sabha): Village-level general assembly of all persons registered in the 
village electoral rolls. 
 
Art. 243B (Three-Tier System & Exemption): Mandatory 3-tier structure; Intermediate 
tier (Panchayat Samiti) is optional for States with a population ≤20 Lakhs. 
 
Art. 243C & 243R (Composition & Age): State Legislature regulates composition; 
minimum qualifying age is 21 years (for both Panchayats and Municipalities). 
 
Art. 243D & 243T (Reservations): Mandatory reservation of not less than 1/3rd (≥33%) 
of total seats and chairpersons for women. 
 
Art. 243E & 243U (Tenure & Dissolution): Fixed term of 5 years; if dissolved 
prematurely, elections must be held within 6 months (not required if remaining term is 
< 6 months). 
 
Art. 243G & 243W (Powers & Responsibilities): Powers over economic development, 
social justice, sanitation, public health, local utilities, and roads/bridges. 
 
Art. 243-I & 243-Y (State Finance Commission): Constituted every 5 years by the 
Governor to review local finance distribution. 
 
Art. 243J & 243Z (Accounts & Audit): State Legislature provides for maintenance and 
audit of accounts. 
 
Art. 243K & 243ZA (State Election Commission): Superintendence, direction, and 
conduct of local elections. 
Traps: 
 
Functional Domain Trap: Local Self-Government includes public health, sanitation, 
water supply, and rural development; Maintenance of Public Order and Judicial Review 
are NOT local-government functions. 
 
Gram Sabha vs Gram Panchayat: Gram Sabha is the entire electorate (body of 
registered voters); Gram Panchayat is the elected executive body. 
 
Audit Authority Trap: Panchayat audit laws are enacted by the State Legislature (NOT 
the Union Parliament, CAG, or District Collector). 
 
Intermediate Level Exemption: Populated threshold where intermediate tier is optional 
is 20 Lakhs.

sheets.heading: Terminology
sheets.text:
Terminology  
Parliamentary Sittings, Sessions & Procedures 
 
Summoning: The President calls each House of Parliament to meet under Article 85; the 
maximum gap between two sessions cannot exceed 6 months. 
 
Session: The period between the first sitting of a House and its prorogation or 
dissolution (Standard sessions: Budget, Monsoon, Winter). 
 
Sitting: A daily meeting of the House during a session (comprises morning and post-
lunch sittings). 
 
Adjournment: Terminates a daily sitting for a specified time (hours, days, or weeks); 
exercised by the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman). 
 
Adjournment Sine Die: Terminating a sitting without assigning a day for reassembly. 
 
Prorogation: Terminates a session of the House (not the House itself); issued by the 
President under Article 85(2). 
 
Dissolution: Ends the life of the House entirely; applies only to Lok Sabha (Rajya Sabha 
is a permanent House). 
 
Recess: The period between the prorogation of a session and the commencement of a 
new session (e.g., when Parliament is in recess, the President may issue ordinances 
under Art. 123). 
 
Quorum: The minimum number of members required to be present to conduct official 
business (1/10th of total membership of the House under Art. 100). 
 
Question Hour: The first hour of every sitting dedicated to asking and answering 
questions. 
 
Zero Hour: An Indian parliamentary innovation (since early 1960s) following Question 
Hour to raise urgent public matters without prior formal notice. 
 
Closure Motion: A motion moved to cut short debate and put the matter directly to 
vote. 
 
Guillotine: A specific form of closure where, upon the expiry of allotted time, all 
undiscussed clauses or demands for grants are put to vote immediately.
