Financial Terms & Cut Motions 
 
Annual Financial Statement: Constitutional nomenclature for the Union Budget under 
Article 112. 
 
Appropriation Bill (Art. 114): Statutory authorization enabling withdrawal of money 
from the Consolidated Fund of India for voted grants and charged expenditure. 
 
Vote on Account (Art. 116): Advance grant given by Lok Sabha to cover estimated 
expenditure for a part of the financial year pending budget passage. 
 
Vote of Credit: An unexpected, blank-check financial grant for an emergency or 
indefinite demand whose details cannot be stated in a budget. 
 
Charged Expenditure: Non-votable expenditure paid directly out of the Consolidated 
Fund of India (can only be discussed). 
 
The Three Cut Motions: 
o Policy Cut: Move to reduce the demand to ₹1 (expresses complete disapproval 
of the underlying policy). 
o Economy Cut: Move to reduce the demand by a specified amount (demands 
economy in expenditure). 
o Token Cut: Move to reduce the demand by ₹100 (ventilates a specific grievance 
within the Government's sphere of responsibility). 
Constitutional Writs & Judicial Concepts 
 
Habeas Corpus ("To have the body"): Quashes illegal or unlawful physical detention. 
 
Mandamus ("We Command"): Directs a public official, inferior court, or statutory 
authority to perform a mandatory public/legal duty. 
 
Prohibition ("To Forbid"): Issued by a higher court to prevent an inferior court or 
tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction (preventive). 
 
Certiorari ("To be Certified"): Issued by a higher court to quash an order already passed 
by an inferior court/tribunal due to lack of jurisdiction or error of law (curative and 
preventive). 
 
Quo-Warranto ("By what warrant/authority"): Inquires into the legality of a person's 
claim to a public office to prevent illegal usurpation. 
 
Judicial Review: Inherent power of constitutional courts to review legislative 
enactments and executive actions against constitutional validity. 
 
Basic Structure Doctrine: Propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973); core structural 
features of the Constitution that cannot be abrogated or destroyed even via Article 368.  
Executive Pardoning Powers (Art. 72 & Art. 161) 
 
Pardon: Completely absorbs and removes both the sentence and conviction, placing the 
offender in the same position as if the offense had never been committed. 
 
Commutation: Substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form (e.g., Death 
sentence -- Rigorous Life Imprisonment).

 

 
 
Remission: Reduces the period/duration of the sentence without changing its 
fundamental character (e.g., 2 years rigorous imprisonment  -- 1 year rigorous 
imprisonment). 
 
Respite: Awards a lesser sentence in place of the original penalty due to special personal 
circumstances (e.g., pregnancy, mental/physical disability). 
 
Reprieve: Grants a temporary stay or postponement of the execution of a sentence 
(especially death penalty) to allow time to seek Presidential pardon. 
Electoral Systems & Federal Governance Terms 
 
First-Past-the-Post (FPTP): Plurality voting system where the candidate securing the 
highest number of valid votes is declared elected (absolute majority >50% not required). 
 
Proportional Representation by Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV): Multi-preference 
quota-based indirect voting system used for President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha, and 
Legislative Councils to ensure proportional representation. 
 
Delimitation: The statutory process of redrawing territorial constituency boundaries 
based on recent census figures to enforce equal representation. 
 
Dyarchy ("Double Rule"): System introduced in provinces under the GoI Act, 1919, 
splitting administrative subjects into Reserved (Governor + Executive Council) and 
Transferred (Governor + Popular Ministers). 
 
Collective Responsibility (Art. 75(3)): Principle that the Council of Ministers is 
collectively answerable to the popular House (Lok Sabha); all ministers sink or swim 
together. 
Traps  
 
Adjournment vs Prorogation vs Dissolution: 
o Adjournment terminates a Sitting (Speaker/Presiding Officer). 
o Prorogation terminates a Session (President/Governor). 
o Dissolution terminates the House (President/Governor). 
 
Cut Motion Amounts: Policy Cut = ₹1 | Token Cut = ₹100 | Economy Cut = Specified 
amount. 
 
Right to Vote: It is a Legal/Statutory Right, not a Fundamental Right. 
 
Local Self-Government Exemption: 3-tier Panchayati Raj applies everywhere, but the 
Intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti) is optional in States with a population of ≤20 
Lakhs.

sheets.heading: State Legislative Assembly
sheets.text:
State Legislative Assembly  
 
Constitutional Status: Governed under Part VI (Articles 168–212); Article 168 provides 
that the State Legislature consists of the Governor + Legislative Assembly (+ Legislative 
Council in bicameral States). 
 
Nature: The Lower, popular House directly elected by citizens on the basis of Universal 
Adult Suffrage (Art. 326) via the First-Past-the-Post (FPTP) system. 
 
Electoral Authority: Elections to the State Legislative Assembly are conducted by the 
Election Commission of India (Art. 324), NOT the State Election Commission. 
 
Collective Responsibility (Art. 164(2)): The State Council of Ministers is collectively 
responsible specifically to the Legislative Assembly. 
Composition, Numbers & Qualifications (Art. 170 & 173) 
 
Strength Limits (Art. 170): Maximum = 500 members; Minimum standard floor = 60 
members. 
 
State Extremes: 
o Largest Assembly: Uttar Pradesh (403 members). 
o Smallest State Assembly: Sikkim (32 members) (Special constitutional 
exception). 
o Smallest UT Assembly: Puducherry (33 members). 
 
Age Qualification (Art. 173): Minimum 25 years for Legislative Assembly (vs. 30 years 
for Legislative Council). 
 
Reservations: 
o Art. 332: Mandatory reservation of seats for SCs and STs based on population 
ratios. 
o 104th CAA (2020): Ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Art. 
333. 
o 106th CAA (2023): Provides approx 1/3rd reservation for women in directly 
elected Assembly seats (effective after post-census delimitation).

Presiding Officers  
 
Speaker & Deputy Speaker (Art. 178): Elected by the Assembly from among its 
members. 
 
Resignation (Art. 179): The Speaker submits resignation to the Deputy Speaker; Deputy 
Speaker resigns to the Speaker. 
 
Continuation After Dissolution (Universal Trap): When the Assembly is dissolved, the 
Speaker does NOT vacate office immediately; continues in office until immediately 
before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly. 
 
Voting: Speaker cannot vote in the first instance, but exercises a casting vote in case of 
an equality of votes (tie). 
 
Disqualification Deciding Authority (Art. 192 vs 10th Schedule): 
o Ordinary Disqualifications (Art. 191/192): Decided by the Governor, who must 
obtain and act according to the binding opinion of the Election Commission of 
India. 
o Defection Disqualifications (10th Schedule): Decided exclusively by the Speaker 
(subject to judicial review). 
Legislative Procedure & Governor's Interface 
 
Sessions & Dissolution (Art. 174): The Governor summons, prorogues, and dissolves the 
Assembly (maximum session gap: 6 months). 
 
Governor's Address (Art. 176): Addressed at the commencement of the first session 
after each general election and the first session of each year. 
 
Money Bills (Arts. 198 & 199): Introduced only in the Assembly with prior 
recommendation of the Governor (Art. 207); Speaker's certification is final; Legislative 
Council has 14 days. 
 
Ordinary Bills (Art. 197): Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for a maximum of 
4 months (3 months first time + 1 month second time); Council cannot permanently 
block legislation. 
 
Assent & Reservation (Arts. 200 & 201): Governor can give assent, withhold assent, 
return an ordinary Bill (no fixed time limit), or reserve the Bill for Presidential 
consideration. 
 
Ordinance Power (Art. 213): Promulgated during legislative recess; ceases to operate 6 
weeks after the reassembly of the State Legislature unless approved earlier. 
 
Ministry Size & Non-Member Ministers (Art. 164): 
o Council of Ministers capped at max 15% of Assembly strength (91st CAA, 2003); 
minimum 12 ministers (including CM). 
o A non-member minister can hold office for a maximum of 6 consecutive months 
without getting elected.

Article 169 (Council Creation/Abolition): Initiated by Assembly passing a resolution by 
Special Majority (majority of total membership + ≥2/3 present and voting) enacted 
into law by Parliament by Simple Majority. 
 
6 Bicameral States: Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, 
and Telangana. 
 
Term Extension during National Emergency: Parliament can extend the Assembly term 
for 1 year at a time, up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases.

Writs    
 
Constitutional Basis: Prerogative remedies borrowed from English common law; issued 
by the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226). 
 
Heart and Soul of the Constitution: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar designated Article 32 as the 
"heart and soul of the Constitution" because it guarantees a direct, effective 
Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies. 
 
Scope Comparison (Universal Trap): 
o Supreme Court (Art. 32): Narrower jurisdiction—issues writs ONLY for the 
enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Part III). 
o High Courts (Art. 226): Wider jurisdiction—issues writs for Fundamental Rights 
AND for any other purpose (enforcement of ordinary statutory/legal rights). 
 
Article 32(3): Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within its 
local jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court.

sheets.heading: Union Minister
sheets.text:
Union Minister   
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V (Articles 74, 75, 77, 78); the Council 
of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head aids and advises the President of India. 
 
Appointment (Art. 75(1)): Prime Minister is appointed by the President; other Union 
Ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. 
 
Tenure (Art. 75(2)): Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (Trap: 
Legally holds office during the pleasure of the President, NOT the Prime Minister). 
 
Oath: The President administers both the Oath of Office and Oath of Secrecy under the 
Third Schedule. 
 
Executive Head vs Head of State: Executive power is constitutionally vested in the 
President (Head of State) under Art. 53; the Prime Minister is the Head of Government. 
Membership & Parliamentary Rights (Art. 75(5) & Art. 88) 
 
House Membership: A Union Minister can be a member of either Lok Sabha or Rajya 
Sabha (No requirement to be a Lok Sabha member). 
 
Non-Member Ministers: A person who is not a member of either House can be 
appointed as a Minister, but must become a member within 6 consecutive months; 
otherwise, ceases to be a Minister (Art. 75(5)). 
 
Speaking vs Voting Rights (Art. 88 Trap): 
o Right to speak and participate in proceedings of both Houses & Joint Sittings -- 
YES 
o Right to vote in the House of which the Minister is NOT a member -- NO (Can 
vote ONLY in the House where they hold membership).

o The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible ONLY to the Lok Sabha (NOT

administrative/bureaucratic lapses under their respective portfolios.

o Union (Art. 75(1A)): Total number of Union Ministers, including the PM, cannot

Deputy Prime Minister Post: An extra-constitutional / non-constitutional post created 
for political convenience; carries the status of a Cabinet Minister without superior 
prime-ministerial powers (First Deputy PM: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, 1947–1950).

sheets.heading: Collegium System
sheets.text:
Collegium System   
 
Core Mandate: The institutional system governing the appointment and transfer of 
judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. 
 
Origin & Status: It is NOT a constitutional body (not expressly mentioned in the 
Constitution) and was NOT created by an Act of Parliament—it is a judicially evolved 
system developed through Supreme Court rulings. 
 
Appointing Authority (Art. 124(2) & 217(1)): Judges are formally appointed by the 
President of India based on the binding recommendations of the Collegium. 
 
Functional Scope: Covers both Appointments (Supreme Court & High Courts) and 
Transfers (High Court Judges). 
Evolution: The Three Judges Cases Chain 
 
First Judges Case (1981 – S.P. Gupta v. Union of India): Held that "consultation" does 
NOT mean "concurrence"; established Executive primacy in judicial appointments. 
 
Second Judges Case (1993 – SCAORA v. Union of India): Reversed the 1981 ruling; held 
that "consultation" means concurrence; established Judicial primacy and formally 
birthed the Collegium system (1993). 
 
Third Judges Case (1998 – Presidential Reference): Clarified procedural working; 
established that the CJI's opinion must reflect a plural consultation with senior 
colleagues (expanded the SC Collegium).

sheets.heading: Scheduled Areas
sheets.text:
Scheduled Areas    
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part X (Article 244(1)) and the Fifth 
Schedule for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. 
 
Declaring Authority: The President of India declares and notifies an area as a Scheduled 
Area  
 
Scope of State Executive Power: Declaration of a Scheduled Area does NOT make it a 
Union Territory, create a separate state, or terminate the State Government's executive 
power—State executive power continues to extend over Scheduled Areas subject to the 
Fifth Schedule. 
Institutional Governance & Governor's Special Powers 
 
Tribal Advisory Council (TAC): Mandatory advisory body established in each State 
having Scheduled Areas (under Paragraph 4 of the Fifth Schedule) to advise on matters 
pertaining to the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes. 
 
Governor's Annual Report: The Governor submits a report regarding the administration 
of Scheduled Areas directly to the President of India (annually or whenever required by 
the President). 
o Trap: It is submitted by the Governor to the President, NOT by the Chief 
Minister to the Union Home Ministry. 
 
Protection of Tribal Land (Paragraph 5): The Governor is empowered to make 
regulations prohibiting or restricting the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals and 
regulating money-lending to STs. 
 
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) Landmark Ruling: The Supreme Court held 
that the transfer/lease of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private parties for mining 
operations is null, void, and inoperative under the Fifth Schedule.

sheets.text:
Judicial Review   
 
Definition: The inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the 
constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders, declaring them void if 
they contravene constitutional provisions. 
 
Exercising Authority: Vested jointly in the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High 
Courts (Article 226) (NOT the Supreme Court alone). 
 
Borrowed Source: Adopted from the USA (originated in Marbury v. Madison, 1803 by 
Chief Justice John Marshall). 
 
Constitutional Supremacy vs. Parliamentary Sovereignty: 
o India: Constitutional Supremacy with Judicial Review. 
o UK: Parliamentary Sovereignty (No traditional judicial review of primary 
parliamentary legislation).

Judicial Review, Basic Structure & 9th Schedule 
 
Basic Structure Integration: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and reaffirmed in Minerva 
Mills (1980), Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was declared an integral part of 
the Basic Structure of the Constitution; Parliament cannot abrogate it even via Article 
368. 
 
Review of Constitutional Amendments: Constitutional amendments are themselves 
subject to Judicial Review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine. 
 
The 9th Schedule Shield (1st CAA, 1951): 
o Added Articles 31A, 31B, and the 9th Schedule to insulate agrarian and land-
reform laws from judicial review on Fundamental Rights grounds. 
o Enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting state 
welfare/land acquisition measures. 
Imp 
 
What Judicial Review is NOT: 
o It is NOT the court questioning the political wisdom, policy merits, or advisability 
of legislation. 
o It is NOT automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills. 
o It is NOT an ordinary appellate proceeding. 
 
Federal vs. Unitary Classification Trap: 
o Judicial Review reinforces the Federal principle (preserves constitutional 
distribution of powers and enforces constitutional limits). 
o It is NOT a Unitary element (unlike All India Services, Governor's appointment, or 
emergency provisions).

Representation of the People Acts (RPA 1950 & 1951)   
 
Key Distinction: 
o RPA, 1950: Deals with the allocation of seats, delimitation of constituencies, 
voter qualifications, preparation of electoral rolls, and the detailed composition 
of State Legislative Councils (Art. 171(2)  ↔ Section 10 & 3rd Schedule of RPA 
1950). 
o RPA, 1951: Deals with the actual conduct of elections, 
qualifications/disqualifications of candidates, registration of political parties, 
corrupt practices, election petitions, and disputes. 
 
Party Registration & Recognition: Political parties are registered by the Election 
Commission of India (ECI) under Section 29A of RPA 1951; recognized as National/State 
parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 (NOT by 
Parliament, Law Ministry, or President). 
 
Right to Vote & Right to Contest: Established as Legal / Statutory Rights (Kuldip Nayar 
v. Union of India, 2006), NOT Fundamental Rights.

Key Legislative Amendments & Candidature Rules 
 
Section 33(7) of RPA, 1951 (Contesting Seat Limits): 
o A candidate can contest from a maximum of 2 Parliamentary or 2 Assembly 
constituencies at a time. 
o Origin & Context: Following the 1991 elections where Devi Lal contested from 3 
Lok Sabha seats, RPA 1951 was amended in 1996 (capping the limit at 2). 
 
Rajya Sabha Domicile / Voter Requirement (2003 Amendment): 
o Prior to 2003, a candidate contesting for Rajya Sabha had to be an elector in that 
particular State. 
o The 2003 Amendment removed this requirement; any registered elector in India 
can contest from any State. Upheld by the SC in Kuldip Nayar (2006). 
 
Death of a Contesting Candidate (1996 Amendment): 
o Elections are no longer countermanded automatically upon the death of a 
candidate; recognized political parties are permitted to nominate a replacement 
within a set timeframe. 
 
Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990): Set up on Electoral Reforms; recommended state 
funding of elections, EVMs, and the measures subsequently enacted in the 1996 RPA 
Amendment. 
 
Delimitation Commission & Electoral Technology  
 
Delimitation Commission: 
o Constituted by the Central Government under an Act of Parliament (headed by a 
retired SC Judge + CEC + State SECs). 
o Finality of Orders: Orders have the force of law and cannot be called in question 
in any court (Art. 329). When laid before Parliament/Assemblies, orders cannot 
be modified. 
o Four Delimitation Commissions constituted so far: 1952, 1963, 1973, and 2002. 


 

 
o VVPAT First Use: Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland (September 2013). 
o NOTA Introduction: Directed by Supreme Court on 27 September 2013 (PUCL v. 
Union of India). 
Imp  
 
Party Registration Authority: Always eliminate options attributing political party 
registration to the Ministry of Law & Justice or Parliament It is strictly executed by the 
Election Commission of India (ECI). 
 
National Party Criteria: 
 A political party must win at least 6% of the total valid votes in four or more 
states during a Lok Sabha (Lok Sabha general election) or State Legislative 
Assembly election, AND it must also win at least 4 Lok Sabha seats from any 
state or states. 
 Alternatively, a party must win at least 2% of the total seats in the Lok Sabha 
(which equals 11 seats), and these elected members must come from at least 3 
different states. 
 Alternatively, a party must be officially recognized as a State Party in at least 4 
different states. 
 
 
Model Code of Conduct (MCC): Comes into force immediately upon the formal 
announcement of the election schedule by the ECI.

sheets.heading: Political Party
sheets.text:
Political Party 
Political Parties & Anti-Defection Dynamics (10th Schedule) 
 
Merger Protection Exception: Disqualification on grounds of defection does not apply if 
a party merges with another and ≥ 2/3rd of the members of the legislative party agree 
to the merger (The original 1/3rd "split" exemption was omitted by the 91st CAA, 2003). 
 
Scope of Disqualification: Applies to members voluntarily giving up party membership 
or voting/abstaining contrary to party whips without prior permission. 
Historical Timeline of Political Parties & Splits 
 
1885: Indian National Congress (INC; First President: W.C. Banerjee). 
 
1925: Communist Party of India (CPI). 
 
1951: Bharatiya Jana Sangh (BJS; Founder: Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee). 
 
1964: CPI Split -- Formation of Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)]. 
 
1980: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP; First President: Atal Bihari Vajpayee; successor to 
BJS). 
 
1984: Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP). 
 
1992: Samajwadi Party (SP). 
 
1998: All India Trinamool Congress (AITC / TMC). 
 
1999: Nationalist Congress Party (NCP; split from INC by Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma, 
Tariq Anwar). 
Key Political Science Concepts & Leader of Opposition (LoP) 
 
"One-Party Dominant System" / "Congress System": Term coined by political scientist 
Rajni Kothari to characterize India's democratic, multi-party electoral landscape 
dominated by the Congress party post-independence. 
 
End of the "Congress System": Marked by the 1989 General Election (ushering in the 
era of minority/coalition governments; V.P. Singh led National Front with outside 
support from BJP + Left). 
 
Leader of Opposition (LoP) Recognition: 
o First formally recognized in 1969. 
o Numerical Threshold: The largest opposition party must hold ≥ 10% of the total 
House strength (approx 55 seats in Lok Sabha). 
  


 

 
 Traps: 
 
 
Merger Fraction Trap: Protection from defection requires agreement of 2/3rd 
members, NOT 1/3rd (1/3rd is the obsolete split threshold). 
 
Constitutional Recognition: Parties were NOT part of the original 1950 text; introduced 
via 52nd CAA, 1985 (10th Schedule). 
 
National Party Threshold: Requires ≥ 6% votes in 4 States + 4 Lok Sabha seats (both 
conditions mandatory under Route 2).

Three Budget Cut Motions (Demands for Grants) 
 
Policy Cut Motion: Move to reduce the demand to ₹1 (Represents complete disapproval 
of the underlying policy). 
 
Economy Cut Motion: Move to reduce the demand by a specified amount (Aims at 
achieving administrative economy). 




control and obliges the Government to resign.





Questions, Calling Attention, or other motions (Written notice to Secretary-General; 
raised from 20 to 30 matters/day in 2015). 
 
Interpellation: The formal procedural right of asking questions to demand explanations



Speaker of Lok Sabha   
 
Constitutional Basis: Governed under Part V (Articles 93–96, 100, 110, 118); 
chosen/elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members (Art. 93). 
 
Membership Requirement: Must already be an elected MP of Lok Sabha at the time of 
election (A non-member cannot be chosen as Speaker under the 6-month relaxation 
rule). 
 
Oath of Office: The Speaker takes NO separate oath of office as presiding officer (Takes 
oath solely as an ordinary Member of Parliament). 
 
Administrative Control: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control 
and guidance of the Speaker.

o Speaker addresses resignation in writing to the Deputy Speaker (Reciprocal: 
Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker). 
o Trap: Resignation goes across laterally, NOT upward to the President. 
 
Effect of Dissolution (Universal Exception Trap):

 

 
o When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker does NOT vacate office 
immediately. 
o Continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly 
elected Lok Sabha. 
 
Removal Mechanism (Art. 94(c)): 
o Removed only by a resolution passed by a majority of ALL THE THEN MEMBERS

o Requires at least 14 days' advance written notice before moving the resolution.

 
Money Bill Certification (Art. 110(4)): Sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is 
a Money Bill; endorsement is final when transmitted to Rajya Sabha and presented to 
the President. 
 
Presiding over Joint Sittings (Art. 118(4)): Presides over joint sittings of both Houses of 
Parliament (In absence: Deputy Speaker Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha). 
 
Maintenance of Order: Adjourns the House or suspends sittings in the absence of a 
Quorum (1/10th strength under Art. 100); exercises Adjournment Sine Die. 
 
Anti-Defection Disqualifications: Decides questions of member disqualification arising 
out of defection under the 10th Schedule (Subject to judicial review per Kihoto 
Hollohan). 
 
Fixing Deputy Speaker Election: The Speaker fixes the date for the election of the 
Deputy Speaker under Rule 8(1).

sheets.heading: Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha
sheets.text:
Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha    
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V (Articles 93–96); chosen/elected by 
the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members (Art. 93). 
 
Election Date Authority (Rule 8(1)): The date of election of the Deputy Speaker is fixed 
by the Speaker of Lok Sabha (communicated to all members by the Secretary-General). 
 
Constitutional Status vs Convention: 
o The Constitution does NOT mandate that the Deputy Speaker must belong to the 
Opposition. 
o Selection of the Deputy Speaker from the Opposition is a parliamentary 
convention/practice, NOT a mandatory constitutional requirement. 
 
Oath of Office: Like the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker takes NO separate oath of office 
as presiding officer (takes oath solely as an ordinary MP).

Powers & Privileges While Presiding (Art. 95) 
 
Equality of Powers: When presiding over a sitting of the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Speaker 
exercises the same powers as the Speaker. 
 
Finality of Rulings: There is no appeal to the Speaker against any ruling given by the 
Deputy Speaker while in the Chair. 
 
Joint Sittings (Art. 118(4)): Presides over Joint Sittings of Parliament if the Speaker is 
absent. 
 
Parliamentary Committees: If appointed to any Parliamentary Committee, the Deputy 
Speaker automatically becomes its Chairman. 
Floor Rights: Normal Sittings vs Own Removal (Art. 96) 
 
During Normal Proceedings (When NOT in the Chair): 
o Sits as an ordinary member of the House. 
o Can participate in debates, move motions, and vote in the first instance. 
 
During Consideration of Own Removal Resolution (Art. 96): 
o Cannot preside over the sitting even if present in the House. 
o Has the right to speak, participate, and vote in the first instance. 
o Cannot exercise a casting vote in case of an equality of votes (tie).

 
Lateral Resignation Trap: Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker, NOT to the President 
or Prime Minister. 
 
Dissolution Protection Distinction: The special constitutional protection to continue 
holding office after the dissolution of Lok Sabha applies only to the Speaker, NOT the 
Deputy Speaker. 
 
Removal Majority: Requires a majority of all the then members of Lok Sabha (Effective 
Majority), NOT a Simple Majority or 2/3rd Special Majority.

sheets.heading: State Legislative Assembly
sheets.text:
State Legislative Assembly  
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part VI (Articles 168–212); the Legislative 
Assembly is the Lower / Popular House of the State Legislature (Art. 168). 
 
State Legislature Composition (Art. 168): 
o Unicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly. 
o Bicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council. 
 
Electoral System: Directly elected by the people from single-member territorial 
constituencies based on Universal Adult Suffrage (Art. 326) using the First-Past-the-
Post (FPTP) system conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI). 
o FPTP Trap: A candidate does NOT need an absolute majority (>50%); the 
candidate securing the highest number of valid votes wins. 
 
Presiding Officers (Art. 178): Speaker and Deputy Speaker are chosen/elected by the 
Assembly from amongst its own sitting members.

 
General Limits (Art. 170): Maximum = 500 seats | Minimum = 60 seats. 
 
Superlatives & Exceptions: 
o Largest State Assembly: Uttar Pradesh (403 seats). 
o Smallest State Assembly: Sikkim (32 seats) (Other small states: Goa = 40, 
Mizoram = 40). 
o Smallest UT Assembly: Puducherry (33 seats) (30 elected + 3 nominated). 
 
SC/ST Seat Reservation (Art. 332): Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes in every State Legislative Assembly in proportion to their population 
in the State. 
Legislative Powers: Money Bills vs Ordinary Bills 
 
State Money Bills (Art. 198 & 199): 
o Can originate ONLY in the Legislative Assembly on the prior recommendation of 
the Governor (Art. 207). 
o The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly has sole and final authority to certify 
whether a Bill is a Money Bill. 
o Legislative Council must return the Bill within 14 days; Assembly can accept or 
reject recommendations. 
 
Ordinary Bills & Council Delay Power (Art. 197 Trap): 
o When an Assembly passes an ordinary Bill and transmits it to the Council: 
 
First Instance: Council can delay up to 3 Months. 


Month. 
o Total Maximum Delay: 4 Months (3 + 1 Months). 
o Trap: The State Council has no veto power and cannot permanently block an 
ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly.

 

 
Tenure, Dissolution & Disqualification Mechanisms 
 
Term & Emergency Extension (Art. 172): Normal term is 5 years; during a National 
Emergency (Art. 352), Parliament may extend the Assembly's duration by law for 1 year 
at a time, up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases. 
 
Summoning & Dissolution (Art. 174): The Governor summons, prorogues, and dissolves 
the Legislative Assembly. 
 
Member Disqualifications (Art. 191 & 192): 
o Grounds include holding an office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged 
insolvent, or loss of citizenship (Art. 191). 
o Deciding Authority (Art. 192): The Governor decides disqualification questions, 
but MUST obtain the opinion of the Election Commission of India (ECI) and act 
according to such opinion. 
  Traps: 
 
Article 169 Resolution Trap: An Assembly resolution recommending the creation or 
abolition of a Legislative Council requires a Special Majority (≥ 50 %total membership + 
≥ 2/3 rdpresent and voting), but does NOT compel the Union Government to introduce 
a Bill in Parliament. 
 
Bicameral States Snapshot (6 States): Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, 
Karnataka, and Uttar Pradesh. 
 
Disqualification Deciding Head: Disqualifications under Art. 191 are decided by the 
Governor acting on ECI's binding advice (Anti-defection under 10th Schedule is decided 
by the Speaker).

sheets.heading: Consolidated Fund & Financial Funds
sheets.text:
Consolidated Fund & Financial Funds   
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part XII (Articles 265–267) and Part V 
(Articles 112–116). 
 
Composition of Consolidated Fund (Art. 266(1)): 
1. All revenues received by the Government (taxes, duties, non-tax revenue). 
2. All loans raised by the Government (treasury bills, market loans, foreign loans). 
3. All moneys received in repayment of loans. 
 
Withdrawal Authority (Universal Rule): No money can be withdrawn from the 
Consolidated Fund of India except under appropriation made by law passed by 
Parliament (Article 114 – Appropriation Act). 
o Trap: Neither the President, Prime Minister, Finance Minister, nor the CAG can 
authorize withdrawals from the CFI on their own authority.

Charged vs. Voted Expenditure on the Consolidated Fund 
 
Charged Expenditure (Non-Votable): 
o Can be discussed by both Houses of Parliament, but is NOT submitted to the 
vote of Parliament. 
o Guaranteed by the Constitution to maintain the financial independence of 
constitutional offices. 
 
Expenditures Specifically Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)): 
o Emoluments and allowances of the President and office expenses. 
o Salaries, allowances, and pensions of the Chairman & Deputy Chairman of Rajya 
Sabha, and Speaker & Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha. 
o Salaries, allowances, and pensions of Judges of the Supreme Court. 
o Pensions ONLY of High Court Judges (Classic    Trap). 
o Salary, allowances, and pensions of the Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India (CAG). 
o Debt charges for which the Government of India is liable (interest, sinking fund 
charges). 
o Any sum required to satisfy any judgment, decree, or arbitral award against the 
Government of India. 
Who is NOT Charged on the CFI? 
 
Vice-President's Salary: The Vice-President receives NO salary as Vice-President; salary 
is drawn in the capacity of Chairman of Rajya Sabha (which is charged). 
 
Prime Minister & Union Ministers: Salaries and allowances of the Prime Minister and 
other Ministers are VOTABLE (NOT charged). 
 
Election Commission of India (ECI): Salaries and administrative expenses of CEC and 
Election Commissioners are NOT charged on the CFI (Source PYQ distinction). 
 
High Court Judges (The Dual-Fund Trap): 
o Salaries & Allowances: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 
202(3)). 
o Pensions: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)(d)(iii)). 
 
Governor's Emoluments: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State. 


 

 
Constitutional Financial Article Chain 
 
Article 265: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law. 
 
Article 266: Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts (Union and States). 
 
Article 267: Contingency Fund (Union and States). 
 
Article 112: Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget). 
 
Article 113: Procedure in Parliament with respect to estimates (Demands for Grants). 
 
Article 114: Appropriation Bills (Authority for withdrawal from CFI). 
 
Article 115: Supplementary, Additional, or Excess Grants. 
 
Article 116: Vote on Account, Votes of Credit, and Exceptional Grants.

Bicameral Legislature & State Legislative Council   
 
Constitutional Basis: Governed under Part VI (Articles 168–212). 
 
State Legislature Structure (Art. 168): 
o Bicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly (Lower House) + Legislative 
Council (Upper House). 
o Unicameral States: Governor + Legislative Assembly. 
 
Current 6 Bicameral States: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, 
Karnataka, and Uttar Pradesh (Largest Council: Uttar Pradesh with 100 seats). 
 
Historical Origin: Bicameralism was first introduced in India at the Central level by the 
Government of India Act, 1919 (Council of State and Central Legislative Assembly).

Creation & Abolition Mechanism (Article 169) 
1. State Assembly Resolution: Initiated by the State Legislative Assembly passing a 
resolution by a Special Majority (≥ 50 %of total membership AND ≥ 2/3 rdof members 
present and voting). 
2. Parliamentary Law: Enacted by Parliament by a Simple Majority (like an ordinary bill). 
3. Article 368 Exclusion: The creation or abolition of a Legislative Council is NOT deemed 
an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. 
4. Trap: The State Assembly resolution is recommendatory; it does NOT legally compel the 
Union Government to introduce a bill in Parliament. 
Composition & Electoral Quotas (Article 171(3)) 
 
Electoral Breakdown: 
o 1/3rd elected by Local Authorities (Municipalities, District Boards, etc.). 
o 1/3rd elected by the Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs) from non-
MLAs. 
o 1/12th elected by Graduates of ≥ 3 years standing residing in the State. 
o 1/12th elected by Teachers of ≥ 3 years standing in educational institutions 
≥secondary school level. 
o 1/6th nominated by the Governor. 
 
Voting System: Elections are conducted via Proportional Representation by means of 
Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV) under secret ballot. 
 
Governor’s Nomination Fields (5 Categories): 
o Literature, Science, Art, Co-operative Movement, and Social Service. 
o Trap: Co-operative Movement exists under Article 171 for State Councils, but is 
NOT a nomination ground for Rajya Sabha under Article 80. "Industrialists" or 
"Commerce" are NOT valid categories.

 

 
Powers over Legislation: Money Bills vs Ordinary Bills 
 
Money Bills (Art. 198): 
o Can originate ONLY in the Legislative Assembly. 
o Council receives the bill for recommendations only and must return it within 14 
days. 
o Assembly is free to accept or reject any recommendation; bill is deemed passed 
upon expiry of 14 days. 
 
Ordinary Bills & Delaying Powers (Art. 197): 
o Council has no veto power and cannot permanently block legislation passed by 
the Assembly. 
o First Passage: Council can delay the bill for a maximum of 3 Months. 
o Second Passage (Re-passed by Assembly): Council can delay for a maximum of 1 
Month. 
o Total Maximum Delaying Period: 4 Months (3 + 1 Months). 
  Traps: 
 
Dissolution vs Abolition Trap: 
o Statement claiming "Legislative Council can be dissolved on the recommendation 
of the Governor" - FALSE (It is a permanent body). 
o Statement claiming "Legislative Council cannot be abolished" - FALSE (Can be 
abolished under Art. 169). 
 
Chairman Selection Trap: The Chairman of the Legislative Council is chosen/elected by 
the Council members from among themselves (Art. 182)—the Governor does NOT 
nominate the Chairman.

sheets.heading: Citizenship & Part II
sheets.text:
Citizenship & Part II   
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part II (Articles 5–11); primarily identified 
citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950). 
 
Exclusive Legislative Authority (Art. 11): Parliament has the exclusive constitutional 
power to regulate citizenship, acquisition, and termination by law (Enacted the 
Citizenship Act, 1955; Citizenship Rules under Section 18). 
o Trap: State Legislatures, the President, or the Election Commission have no 
power to make citizenship laws. 
 
Single Citizenship & Single Domicile: India provides for a Single Citizenship and a single 
domicile across the entire territory (a unitary feature of the federal structure; unlike the 
USA which has dual federal and state citizenship).

Acquisition & Loss of Citizenship (Citizenship Act, 1955) 
 
5 Modes of Acquisition (B-D-R-N-I): 
1. Birth: Based on place of birth (Jus soli / modified criteria). 
2. Descent: Born outside India to Indian citizen parents (Jus sanguinis). 
3. Registration (Sec. 5): Person of Indian Origin (PIO) ordinarily resident in India for 
7 years prior to applying; persons married to Indian citizens. 
4. Naturalization (Sec. 6): Granted to foreigners meeting residency and character 
criteria. 
5. Incorporation of Territory: Acquisition of a new territory by India (e.g., Goa, 
Pondicherry, Sikkim). 
 
3 Modes of Loss (R-T-D): 
1. Renunciation: Voluntary surrender of citizenship by an Indian national. 
2. Termination: Automatic loss when an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires the 
citizenship of another country (Art. 9). 
3. Deprivation (Sec. 10): Compulsory termination by the Central Government on 
grounds of fraud, disloyalty to the Constitution, unlawful trading with an enemy 
during war, or imprisonment for ≥ 2 years within 5 years of 
naturalization/registration. 
Traps: 
 
Head of State / Presidential Eligibility Trap: 
o In the USA, only a natural-born citizen can become President. 
o In India, both a citizen by birth AND a naturalized citizen are eligible to become 
President of India (Art. 58). 
 
What Does NOT Acquire Citizenship: 
o Depositing money in Indian banks / purchasing property in India - NO . 
 
What Does NOT Cause Automatic Loss: 
o Marrying a foreign citizen - NO  (Does not by itself revoke citizenship). 
o Criticizing the government or policies - NO

 

 
 
Deprivation of Naturalized Citizens: 
o Statement claiming "A naturalized citizen can never be deprived of citizenship" - 
FALSE  (Can be deprived under Section 10). 
 
Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder (Sec. 7A): 
o Persons who were citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh (or whose 
parents/grandparents belonged to them) are strictly ineligible for OCI 
registration. 
 
Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 (CAA) Passage Milestones: 
o Lok Sabha: Passed on 9 December 2019 -- Rajya Sabha: Passed on 11 December 
2019 -- Presidential Assent: 12 December 2019. 
o Cut-off Date: Applies to 6 non-Muslim persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, 
Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014.

sheets.heading: Sessions of Parliament
sheets.text:
Sessions of Parliament   
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V (Article 85); the President summons 
each House of Parliament at such time and place as they think fit. 
 
Six-Month Rule: The maximum gap between two consecutive sessions cannot exceed 6 
months (Six months shall not intervene between the last sitting in one session and the 
date appointed for the first sitting in the next session). 
 
Constitutional Mandate vs Practice: 
o Constitution mandates that Parliament must meet at least twice a year. 
o The Constitution does NOT specify a fixed number of sessions (having 3 
sessions—Budget, Monsoon, Winter—is a parliamentary convention). 
o The Constitution does NOT prescribe a minimum number of sitting days in a 
year.

 
Session Gap vs Ordinance Lifespan: 
o Maximum interval between two Parliamentary sessions = 6 Months (Art. 85). 
o Maximum validity of an Ordinance after reassembly = 6 Weeks (Art. 123). 
o Maximum possible lifespan of an Ordinance without approval = 6 Months + 6

 
MP Absence vs House Prorogation (Art. 101(4)): 
o An MP's unexcused absence of 60 days can lead to vacation of the seat. 
o Exclusion Rule: Calculation strictly excludes periods of Prorogation and 
Adjournments exceeding 4 consecutive days. 
 
 
Fixed Calendar Fallacy: Any option claiming "The Constitution mandates three sessions: 
Budget, Monsoon, and Winter" - FALSE  (Only the 6-month maximum gap is 
constitutionally mandated). 
 
Minimum Days Trap: Any option stating "Parliament must sit for a minimum of 
60/90/100 days per year" - FALSE  (No minimum days prescribed in the Constitution). 
 
Prorogation & Advice: The President exercises prorogation on the aid and advice of the 
Council of Ministers, not at absolute personal discretion.

Constitutional, Statutory & Extra-Constitutional Bodies    
 
Constitutional Body: An authority or institution directly established, empowered, and 
anchored within the text of the Constitution of India. 


Lokpal, NGT). 
 
Extra-Constitutional / Non-Statutory Body: Established via an Executive Order or 
Cabinet Resolution (e.g., NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC). 
 
Trap: The Planning Commission (1950) and NITI Aayog (2015) are Extra-Constitutional 
Bodies (NOT Constitutional, NOT Statutory).

None of the Above (NOTA)   
 
Definition & Objective: NOTA (None of the Above) is an electoral option provided on 
ballot papers and Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) enabling voters to exercise a 
negative vote and formally reject all contesting candidates in secret.  
 
Judicial Origin: Directed by the Supreme Court of India in the landmark judgment PUCL 
v. Union of India on 27 September 2013.  
 
Constitutional Foundation: The Supreme Court linked the right to register a negative 
vote in secrecy with the Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(1)(a).  
Major Electoral Technology & Reform Milestones 
 
1982: First experimental use of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) in the Parur 
Assembly constituency, Kerala. 
 
1993: Introduction of Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC / Voter ID). 
 
4 September 2013: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) introduced and first used 
experimentally in the Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland. 
 
27 September 2013: Supreme Court directs mandatory introduction of the NOTA button 
on EVMs.

Constitutional Amendment Battle (Art. 368 vs Part III) 
 
Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld the 1st CAA; ruled that ordinary 
law under Art. 13(2) does not include constitutional amendments under Art. 368 
(Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights). 
 
Golaknath (1967): Overruled earlier cases; held that an amendment is "law" under Art. 
13(2) and Parliament cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right. 
 
Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973): Delivered by the largest bench (13 Judges; 7:6 
majority); held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution (including FRs), 
but cannot damage or destroy the "Basic Structure". 
 
Minerva Mills (1980): Reaffirmed that a limited amending power is itself a Basic 
Feature; invalidated clauses (4) and (5) of Art. 368 inserted by the 42nd CAA.

 
Textual Fallacy: Statement claiming "The term 'Basic Structure' is explicitly defined in 
Part XX of the Constitution" - FALSE  (Judicially formulated concept). 


o Statement claiming "Fundamental Rights can never be amended post-
Kesavananda" - FALSE  
o Correct Principle: FRs can be amended, provided the amendment does not 
violate the Basic Structure.

 

 
 
Judicial Review as Basic Structure: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills 
(1980), and L. Chandra Kumar (1997), Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was 
explicitly declared an inviolable part of the Basic Structure. 
 
India vs UK Constitutional Model: 
o India: Constitutional Supremacy + Judicial Review of primary legislation. 
o United Kingdom: Parliamentary Sovereignty (No striking down of primary 
parliamentary statutes).

Seventh Schedule (Union, State & Concurrent Lists)   
 
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part XI (Articles 245–255) and the Seventh 
Schedule, operationalized through Article 246 (Subject distribution) and Article 246A 
(Special provision for GST via 101st CAA, 2016). 
 
Three-Fold Distribution (Article 246): 
o List I (Union List): Parliament has exclusive legislative competence (Art. 246(1)). 
o List II (State List): State Legislatures have exclusive legislative competence (Art. 
246(3)). 
o List III (Concurrent List): Both Parliament and State Legislatures have concurrent 
legislative competence (Art. 246(2)). 
 
Residuary Powers (Article 248): Legislative competence over any subject NOT 
enumerated in any of the three Lists is vested exclusively in Parliament (e.g., Space 
Research, Cyber Law). 
 
Repugnancy Rule (Article 254): In case of conflict between Central and State legislation 
on a Concurrent List subject, the Central law prevails (Unless the State law was reserved 
for Presidential assent and received it under Art. 254(2)).

Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147). 
 
Inauguration & Predecessor: Inaugurated on 28 January 1950; succeeded both the 
Federal Court of India (established under the Government of India Act, 1935) and the 
Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. 
 
Strength & Parliament's Power: The power to increase the number of Supreme Court 
judges is vested exclusively in Parliament by law (Art. 124(1)). 
 
Retirement Age & Removal: Judges retire at 65 years of age (Art. 124(2)); removed by 
the President following an Address supported by a Special Majority in each House of 
Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Art. 124(4)).

Curative Petitions & Special Powers (Articles 141 & 142) 
 
Article 141 (Binding Precedent): The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on 
all courts within the territory of India. 
 
Article 142 (Complete Justice): 
o Empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing 
"Complete Justice" in any cause or matter pending before it. 
o Operates unhindered by ordinary statutory limitations. 
 
Curative Petition (Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra, 2002): 
o Evolved by the Supreme Court under its inherent powers anchored in Article 142 
to prevent abuse of process and cure gross miscarriages of justice after a review 
petition under Article 137 has been dismissed. 
Benches, Courts of Record & Appointment Mechanics 
 
Constitution Bench (Article 145(3)): 
o Minimum 5 Judges required to hear any case involving a substantial question of 
law as to the interpretation of the Constitution or for references under Article 
143. 
 
Court of Record (Article 129 vs Article 215): 
o Supreme Court (Art. 129): Decisions have evidentiary value and cannot be 
questioned in subordinate courts; has inherent power to punish for contempt of 
itself. 
o High Court (Art. 215): Parallel Court of Record status at the State level. 
 
Supreme Court Collegium Framework: 
o Composition: CJI + 4 Senior-most Supreme Court Judges (Total = 5 members). 
o Genesis: Judicially evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1st Case: 1981 -- 
2nd Case: 1993 -- 3rd Case: 1998). 
o Trap: Neither created by an Act of Parliament nor explicitly written in the 
Constitution. 
 


 

 
Imp Traps  
 
Original Jurisdiction Exclusions (Art. 131): Inter-State water disputes (Art. 262), Finance 
Commission matters (Art. 280), and recovery of damages by a private party against the 
Union are NOT covered under Article 131. 
 
SLP Armed Forces Exception (Art. 136(2)): Special Leave Petitions do NOT lie against 
judgments/sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals. 
 
Advisory Opinion Binding Status (Art. 143): Opinions rendered by the Supreme Court to 
the President under Article 143 are strictly advisory and NOT binding on the President.

Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part VI, Chapter V (Articles 214–231); 
Article 214 mandates a High Court for each State.

o 1862: First three High Courts established at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. 
o 1866: High Court for North-Western Provinces established at Agra (shifted to 
Allahabad in 1869). 
 
Strength Determination (Art. 216): The strength/number of judges for each High Court 
is decided and fixed by the President of India (NOT Parliament, NOT the Governor/Chief 
Minister).

Appointment, Eligibility, Transfer & Post-Retirement Rules 
 
Appointment Consultation Matrix (Art. 217): 
o Chief Justice of HC: Appointed by President after consultation with the CJI + 
Governor of the State. 
o Other HC Judges: Appointed by President after consultation with the CJI + 
Governor + Chief Justice of that High Court. 
 
Qualifications (Art. 217(2)): 
o Citizen of India AND 
o Held a judicial office in India for ≥ 10 years OR 
o Practiced as an advocate of a High Court for ≥ 10 years 
o Trap: Unlike the Supreme Court (Art. 124(3)(c)), there is NO provision for 
appointing a "distinguished jurist" as a High Court judge. 
 
Removal Mechanism (Art. 217(1)(b) r/w Art. 124(4)): 
o Removed ONLY by the President following an Address passed by each House of 
Parliament by a Special Majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or 
incapacity. 
 
Post-Retirement Practice (Art. 220): 
o A retired permanent HC Judge CANNOT plead/act before any court or authority 
in India, EXCEPT the Supreme Court and other High Courts (where they did not 
serve as a permanent judge). 
Jurisdiction: Writs (Art. 226) vs Superintendence (Art. 227) 
 
Writ Scope (Art. 226 > Art. 32): 
o High Court writ jurisdiction is broader in scope than the Supreme Court because 
it extends to Fundamental Rights + Any other legal purpose/right. 
o High Court writ power is discretionary; Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right. 
 
Supervisory Jurisdiction (Art. 227): 
o High Court exercises administrative and judicial superintendence over all 
subordinate courts and tribunals throughout its territorial jurisdiction. 
o Armed Forces Exception: Does NOT extend to courts and tribunals constituted 
under any law relating to the Armed Forces (Art. 227(4)). 
Territorial Jurisdiction & Common High Courts (Arts. 230 & 231) 
 
Parliament has the power under Article 231 to establish a Common High Court for two 
or more States and UTs. 
 
Imp Cross-Jurisdictions: 
o Bombay High Court: Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu. 
o Calcutta High Court: West Bengal + Andaman & Nicobar Islands. 
o Kerala High Court: Kerala + Lakshadweep. 
o Madras High Court: Tamil Nadu + Puducherry. 
o Punjab & Haryana High Court: Punjab, Haryana + Chandigarh.

 

 
o Gauhati High Court: Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh. 
Imp Traps 
 
Appointment Head Trap: High Court Judges are appointed by the President of India, 
NOT the Governor. 
 
Oath vs Resignation Head Trap: 
o Oath administered by the Governor of the State (Art. 219). 
o Resignation submitted to the President of India (Art. 217(1)(a)). 
 
Salary vs Pension Source Trap: 
o Salaries & Allowances: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State. 
o Pensions: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Judges of Supreme Court vs. High Court

Constitutional Framework: 
o Supreme Court Judges: Governed under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147). 
o High Court Judges: Governed under Part VI, Chapter V (Articles 214–231). 
 
Appointing Authority (Universal Rule): Both Supreme Court and High Court Judges are 
appointed exclusively by the President of India by warrant under hand and seal (The 
Governor has NO power to appoint High Court Judges). 
 
Resignation Recipient: Both Supreme Court and High Court Judges address their written 
resignations directly to the President of India. 
 
Removal Mechanism: Both SC and HC Judges are removed only by an order of the 
President following an Address by each House of Parliament supported by a Special 
Majority (≥ 50 % total strength + ≥ 2/3 rd present and voting) on the grounds of proved 
misbehaviour or incapacity (Arts. 124(4) & 218).

Acting Chief Justice (Art. 223): Appointed by the President from among HC Judges when

actions), the Chief Justice of a High Court is subject to the writ jurisdiction (Art. 226) of 
another Judge of that same High Court. 


administrative decisions.

(where they were not a permanent judge). 


o High Court Judge's Oath Administered by Governor.

sheets.text:
Tribunals   
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part XIV-A (Articles 323-A & 323-B); 
inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 on the recommendations of 
the Swaran Singh Committee. 
 
Core Nature: Quasi-judicial, specialized dispute resolution bodies created to reduce 
pendency in regular courts and provide domain expertise. 
 
Judicial Review Anchor (L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997): 
o The Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review of the High Courts 
under Article 226/227 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral 
part of the Basic Structure. 
o Clauses excluding the jurisdiction of High Courts and the Supreme Court in 
Articles 323-A and 323-B were declared unconstitutional. 
o Decisions of tribunals (like CAT) are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench 
of the concerned High Court before approaching the Supreme Court.

o Established in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (Article 323-A).

 
Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT): 
o Established under the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000 (Original parent act: TRAI 
Act, 1997). 
o Adjudicates disputes in telecom, broadcasting, and airport tariff matters. 
o Appellate Routes: Telecom/broadcasting/tariff appeals lie directly to the 
Supreme Court on substantial questions of law; cyber appellate orders route to 
the High Court.

o Statutory body established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (Guided 
by principles of Natural Justice, not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908). 
o Appeals against NGT orders lie directly to the Supreme Court (within 90 days).

sheets.text:
Electronic Voting Machines (EVM)   
 
First Experimental Use: 19 May 1982 in the Parur Assembly Constituency, Kerala (A.C. 
Jose v. Sivan Pillai case). 


direction, and control of the Election Commission of India (ECI) for Lok Sabha and State 
Legislative Assembly elections. 


apparatus, NOT an electoral system. India conducts direct general elections using the 
First-Past-the-Post (FPTP) system (where the candidate with the highest valid votes 
wins, irrespective of crossing 50%).

 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Article 123 (President of India) and Article 
213 (Governor of a State).

Nature of Power: The ordinance-making power is a legislative power of the Executive, 
NOT an executive or administrative function. 


both Houses are in session in a bicameral legislature, or the single House in unicameral 
states) and the Head of State is satisfied that circumstances exist requiring immediate 
action. 
 
Co-extensive Scope: An Ordinance has the same force, effect, and limitations as an Act

The Six-Week Rule & Lifespan Calculations 
 
Reassembly Rule: An Ordinance must be laid before Parliament/State Legislature when 
it reassembles and ceases to operate 6 weeks after the date of reassembly unless 
approved earlier. 
 
Different Assembly Dates: If the two Houses reassemble on different dates, the 6-week 
countdown begins from the later of the two dates. 


Parliamentary approval window (6 weeks) = 6 Months and 6 Weeks.

Legislature, NOT the Union Council of Ministers or the President.

Wadhwa (1987) & Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): Re-promulgation of ordinances without 
legislative ratification is a subversion of the Constitution).

sheets.text:
Rule of Law   
 
Philosophical Origin & Jurist: Propounded by British constitutional jurist A.V. Dicey in 
Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885). 
 
Constitutional Origin / Borrowing: Borrowed from the British Constitutional System 
(alongside Parliamentary Government, Single Citizenship, Cabinet System, and 
Prerogative Writs). 
 
Constitutional Anchor in India: Anchored primarily in Article 14 (Equality before Law 
and Equal Protection of the Laws), applying to both citizens and foreigners, and affirmed 
as part of the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973 & Indira Nehru Gandhi, 1975). 
Dicey's 3 Classic 
Elements 
Operational Meaning & Legal Scope

Core Conceptual Distinctions:

 

 
Conceptual Pair 
Core Difference  
Rule of Law vs. Rule by 
Law 
• Rule of Law: Government itself is subordinate to the law; laws 
must be just, fair, and non-arbitrary (Government under Law). 
• Rule by Law: Law is used purely as an instrument/weapon of 
state control to govern citizens while the ruler remains above it 
(Government above Law). 
Equality Before Law vs. 
Equal Protection of 
Laws (Art. 14) 
• Equality Before Law: British origin; negative concept (absence of 
special privilege for any individual). 
• Equal Protection of the Laws: American origin; positive concept 
(equal treatment under equal circumstances / Reasonable 
Classification permitted). 
Procedure Established 
by Law vs. Due Process 
of Law 
• Procedure Established by Law (Art. 21 text): Law is valid if 
enacted following correct legislative procedure (A.K. Gopalan, 
1950). 
• Due Process of Law (Post-Maneka Gandhi, 1978): Law must also 
be "just, fair, and reasonable" and free from procedural 
arbitrariness. 
Constitutional 
Government 
• Synonymous with Limited Government—power is defined, 
restrained, and checked by constitutional provisions to prevent 
executive tyranny. 
Rule of Law vs. Public 
Interest Litigation (PIL) 
•  PIL promotes and strengthens access to justice for the 
disadvantaged, but is NOT an indispensable prerequisite for the 
existence of Rule of Law (Rule of Law existed prior to PIL evolution 
via Arts. 14, 32, and 226). 
Arbitrary Discretion & Article 14  
 
A law that confers on an executive authority an unguided, uncontrolled, and 
uncanalized discretionary power in the matter of application or enforcement violates 
the principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and directly subverts the Rule of Law. 
 
Imp Traps  
 
Trap:

 

 
o Option Component: "People's responsibility to the government"  DELETE (Rule 
of Law restrains the government, not expands citizens' obedience to authority). 
 
Dicey's Third Principle in India: 
o In the UK, the Constitution is the result of judicial decisions on individual rights. 
o In India, the Constitution is the Source of Rights (reversing Dicey's third premise 
while adopting the first two intact). 
 
Administrative Discretion Rule: Executive discretion without objective standards or 
judicial safeguards is ultra vires Article 14.

Pre-Condition Trigger (Art. 334A): The reservation does NOT come into force 
immediately; it will take effect only after a delimitation exercise is conducted following 
the publication of the relevant figures of the first decennial Census conducted post-



extended by Parliament by law).  
 
Rotation of Seats: Reserved seats for women shall be rotated after every subsequent 
delimitation exercise as determined by parliamentary law.  
Panchayats & Municipalities: Sub-Articles & State Enhancements 
 
Article 243D Breakdown (Panchayats): 
o Article 243D(2): Not less than 1/3rd of the total seats reserved for SCs and STs 
shall be reserved for women belonging to SCs/STs (Sub-reservation within 
quota). 
o Article 243D(3): Not less than 1/3rd of the total directly elected seats in every 
Panchayat shall be reserved for women (including SC/ST women).

the village, intermediate, and district levels for women.

o The constitutional baseline is strictly 1/3rd (33.33%). 
o States have statutory discretion to increase this quota: Bihar was the first State 
to grant 50% reservation for women in Panchayats (2006), followed by States 
like Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Himachal Pradesh. 
 
 


 

 
Historical Trends & Electoral Milestones  
 
Lowest Women Representation: 6th Lok Sabha (1977)  Only 19 women MPs elected. 
 
17th Lok Sabha (2019): 78 women MPs elected (approx 14.36% of total strength, the 
highest up to that point).

 
Upper Houses Exclusion Trap: If an exam option states "The 106th Constitutional 
Amendment provides 33% reservation for women in Rajya Sabha and State Legislative 
Councils"  FALSE (Applies exclusively to Lok Sabha, State Assemblies, and Delhi

 
Local Body Minimum Age Trap: The minimum age required to contest 
Panchayat/Municipality elections is 21 years (Art. 243V / 243F), NOT 25 years. 
 
SC/ST Women Proportion Trap: Within SC/ST reserved seats, the mandatory sub-quota 
for SC/ST women is 1/3rd (not 50%).





 
Current Law: Disqualification does not apply if a member's original political party 
merges with another party and not less than two-thirds (2/3rd) of the legislature party

defection matters—it is decided solely by the Speaker/Chairman.

submitting a formal letter of resignation.

o 25 Years: Lower Houses  Lok Sabha + State Legislative Assembly. 
o 30 Years: Upper Houses  Rajya Sabha + State Legislative Council. 
 
The 18 vs 21 Voting vs Contesting Trap: 
o 18 Years: Right to vote under Universal Adult Franchise (Art. 326). 
o 21 Years: Minimum age to contest Panchayat / Municipality elections (Arts. 243F 
/ 243V). 
 
The 35-Year Executive Trio: 
o President (Art. 58) + Vice-President (Art. 66) + Governor (Art. 157) all share the 
exact same minimum age qualification of 35 years.

Constitutional Salaries & Funds   
 
Determining Authority vs. Source Fund: Who determines the salary (Parliament/State 
Legislature by law) is a distinct legal question from which fund pays it (Consolidated 
Fund of India vs. State) and whether it is Charged or Voted. 
 
Constitutional Schedules: 
o Second Schedule: Emoluments, allowances, and privileges of constitutional 
office-holders (President, Governors, Presiding Officers, SC/HC Judges, CAG). 
o Trap Pair: Second Schedule = Salaries  ↔ Third Schedule = Forms of Oaths. 
 
Charged vs. Voted Rule (Arts. 112 & 202): Charged expenditure can be discussed in 
Parliament/State Legislature, but is NOT submitted to vote.

sheets.heading: Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG)
sheets.text:
Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG)   
 
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V, Chapter V (Articles 148–151). 
 
Constitutional Identity: An independent constitutional authority designated as the 
Guardian of the Public Purse / Public Finance and the head of the Indian Audit and 
Accounts Department. 
 
Constitutional Weight: Described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the most important officer 
under the Constitution of India (one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system, 
along with SC, UPSC, and ECI). 
 
Statutory Milestone (1971 / 1976): 
o CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. 
o 1976 Separation Reform: Departmentalization of Union accounts separated 
Accounting from Auditing (CAG was relieved of the responsibility of preparing 
Union accounts with effect from 1 March 1976; continues to compile and 
maintain accounts of most States).

 
Relationship with PAC: CAG acts as the "Friend, Philosopher, and Guide" of the Public 
Accounts Committee (PAC), attending meetings and assisting in the line-by-line 
examination of audit reports. 
 
Initial Report Routing Trap: The CAG does NOT submit reports directly to the PAC or 
Parliament; reports are submitted strictly to the President/Governor first. 
 
Ultimate Enforcing Authority: The ultimate constitutional responsibility for taking 
action on the findings in CAG reports rests with Parliament / State Legislature. 
Imp Traps  
 
Report Submission Destination Trap: 
o Statement claiming "CAG submits audit reports directly to the Public Accounts 
Committee" -- FALSE  (Submitted to President/Governor under Art. 151). 
 
Comptroller vs. Auditor Trap: 
o Statement claiming "CAG ensures no money is drawn from the Consolidated Fund 
of India without prior sanction" -- FALSE  (Audit is post-expenditure / ex-post 
facto). 
 
Form of Accounts Advice Trap (Art. 150): Accounts are kept in the form prescribed by 
the President, upon the advice of the CAG (NOT by the CAG unilaterally). 
 
Post-Retirement Ban: CAG cannot take up any further office under either the Central or 
State Governments (unlike UPSC Chairman, who cannot take another job, or judges who 
can head commissions).
